findings.committee: Economy, Regeneration, Transport and Infrastructure Committee
findings.headline: Second-year ongoing savings target rises to £2.74m, 47% above first-year figure of £1.87m, driven by delayed implementation of new parking and floating bridge charges
findings.detail: The 2027-28 savings are £1.87m; 2028-29 and ongoing are £2.74m. The increase is driven by new on-street and off-street parking charges, which contribute £0 in year one but £405,966 in year two. This suggests material savings are back-loaded or contingent on successful consultation and implementation of new charges.
findings.matters: A finance director would note that the savings plan depends on consultation-dependent proposals delivering in year two. If consultation delays implementation or proposals are modified, the ongoing savings target (£2.74m) is at risk. First-year savings are achievable from existing tariff increases and floating bridge alone, but the step-up is not guaranteed.
findings.quote: New on-street parking charges 2027-28 £0 / 2028-29 £311,166; New off-street parking charges 2027-28 £0 / 2028-29 £94,900; Total 2027-28 £1,870,239; Total 2028-29 onwards £2,737,384

findings.committee: Economy, Regeneration, Transport and Infrastructure Committee
findings.headline: Highways PFI review proposals are explicitly acknowledged to create "future financial risk due to reduced standards"
findings.detail: The highways PFI contract review (rated 1 red and 2 amber, not fully green) proposes multiple cost reductions: street lighting dimming, removing vegetation maintenance from structures, changes to road quality inspection thresholds, and removal of traffic management for community events. The council's own assessment states these changes will result in future financial risk and notes reputational risk and need for police consultation on CCTV.
findings.matters: A finance officer elsewhere or a lender would flag that these savings create documented future financial liabilities. The proposal trades present savings for future costs, and deferred maintenance risk often materializes. The mixed deliverability ratings (not all green) suggest internal uncertainty about implementation.
findings.quote: Some of these proposals will result in future financial risk due to reduced standards

findings.committee: Economy, Regeneration, Transport and Infrastructure Committee
findings.headline: Museum closure to save £21.5k will block Mend grant application for Guildhall refurbishment
findings.detail: The museums review (rated red) proposes closure of the Museum of Island History, with a consequence explicitly flagged: the closure will prevent the council from proceeding with a Mend grant application to refurbish the Guildhall. The council notes it will still need to maintain the Roman Villa despite the closure.
findings.matters: The £21.5k saving carries an opportunity cost of lost external funding (size of Mend grant not stated) and ongoing maintenance liability. A finance director would see this as savings that trade one external funding source for obligations elsewhere.
findings.figures: £21,520 (both years)
findings.quote: Also closure of the Museum of Island History located at the Guildhall will mean the Mend grant application for the refurbishment of the Guildhall will not be able to proceed

findings.committee: Economy, Regeneration, Transport and Infrastructure Committee
findings.headline: Library service savings of £81,000 (year one) and £162,000 (ongoing) rated red for deliverability with risks including loss of public health funding partnership
findings.detail: The library services proposal is rated red for deliverability due to multiple external dependencies. The document states in capitals that any reduction in service provision risks losing financial support from public health. The council would also need to repay the library improvement fund for Cowes Library if closed. Legal risk is also noted: loss of service "if Town and Parishes don't support and risk of judicial review."
findings.matters: A finance director would see that a £162k ongoing saving in a red-rated proposal is dependent on a separate public health funding partnership: if that partner withdraws support in response, the council loses both the library savings and the public health funding. This is contingent savings with reverse downside risk.
findings.quote: ANY REDUCTION IN SERVICE PROVISION HAS THE RISK OF IMPACTING (STOPPING OF REDUCING) THE FINANCIAL SUPPORT RECEIVED FROM PUBLIC HEALTH

findings.committee: Economy, Regeneration, Transport and Infrastructure Committee
findings.headline: Two-thirds of 2027-28 savings (£1.23m of £1.87m) come from parking tariff increases and floating bridge fare rises, all rated green but subject to consultation and local opposition
findings.detail: The council is proposing increases to on-street and off-street parking (£315,786 in tariffs alone, plus £91,014 from removing EV free parking), new charges on previously free streets and car parks, and significant floating bridge fare rises (£820,584). These income-based savings dominate the plan and are concentrated in two revenue sources. All are marked green for deliverability but several note reputational risk and expected local opposition campaigns.
findings.matters: A lender would note heavy reliance on demand-sensitive, politically contested revenue rather than efficiency savings, and the risk that consultation or sustained opposition might prevent delivery of a material portion of the plan.
findings.figures: 2027-28 parking tariff increase £315,786; new on-street parking £0 year one / £311,166 ongoing; new off-street parking £0 year one / £94,900 ongoing; remove EV free parking £91,014; floating bridge fares £820,584
findings.quote: Parking tariffs £315,786 / £451,123; Floating Bridge fares £820,584 / £820,584; New on-street parking charges subject to consultation and updating parking strategy; New off-street parking charges subject to consultation

findings.committee: Adult Social Care, Public Health and Housing Needs Committee
findings.headline: Savings delivery is dependent on external training and transformation delivery from NDTi
findings.detail: Multiple proposals reference existing 'work we have been doing with NDTi' and require continued NDTi engagement to deliver outcomes. The supported employment redesign requires NDTi contracting (£15,000 over 2 years), and the practice improvement proposals require NDTi Phase 3 implementation (£75,000 in year 1, £25,000 in year 2). Delivery risk is concentrated in an external partner.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to understand key delivery dependencies. If NDTi engagement is unsuccessful, delayed, or costly beyond budget, the savings timeline and amounts could be affected, creating a budget delivery risk.
findings.figures: £15,000 annual NDTi contract for supported employment (2 years); £100,000 total NDTi investment for practice improvement Phase 3
findings.quote: Transformation funding would be required to build on the work we have been doing with NDTi and implement Phase 3. The investment required would be £75k year 1 + £25k year 2.

findings.committee: Adult Social Care, Public Health and Housing Needs Committee
findings.headline: £656,870 in transformation and capital funding required upfront to deliver the savings proposals
findings.detail: Multiple proposals require investment before savings materialize: day services facility costs (£255,000 from DFG grant), pilot staffing on 2-year contracts (£182,718), NDTi training and implementation over two years (£100,000), and specialist housing and workforce development (£44,576). If transformation funding is unavailable, the proposals cannot proceed and the savings will not be achieved.
findings.matters: The savings plan is conditional on capital availability. If funding depends on external grants (DFG for day services) or cannot be afforded from reserves, the entire savings strategy is at risk. A lender would want to understand this constraint.
findings.figures: £656,870 total capital and transformation requirements; £255,000 for day services; £182,718 for support worker pilots; £100,000 for NDTi training; £44,576 for housing advice and upskilling
findings.quote: Introduce day support services at The Goulding's. Pre-pandemic this was a well-used service that supported local people and reduced strain on unpaid/family carers. This would require capital investment of £225,000 to implement but this would come from ringfenced DFG grant.

findings.committee: Adult Social Care, Public Health and Housing Needs Committee
findings.headline: Service risks accepted in pursuit of savings: community equipment service faces potential delivery delays after grant termination
findings.detail: The council is ending a grant-funded community equipment service (£90k annual saving) and transferring delivery to the in-house Community Equipment Service. The council's impact assessment explicitly flags potential delays in equipment provision. A second contract termination (user-led organisation, £150k saving) requires engagement activities to be absorbed into mainstream ASC 'business as usual' capacity.
findings.matters: Equipment delays could create safeguarding issues and complaints; absorbing activities into BAU risks operational overload. A finance director needs to understand whether the operating model can handle these changes without service deterioration or additional costs elsewhere.
findings.figures: £90,000 annual saving from community equipment grant termination; £150,000 annual saving from user-led organisation contract termination
findings.quote: Determine not to renew the grant to provider which is due to end on 31/03/2027 and is used to support the provision of community equipment. This service will be delivered by the Community Equipment Service.

findings.committee: Adult Social Care, Public Health and Housing Needs Committee
findings.headline: Adult social care savings plan of £10.5m over three years depends on achieving specific outcome improvements through service transformation and staff investment
findings.detail: The proposals aim to reduce care costs by increasing the proportion of people in paid employment from 70 to 91 (30% increase), increasing people living independently from 350 to 455 (30% increase), and reducing supported living placements by 47 people (30% decrease). Achieving these targets requires new staffing (support workers, housing officers, benefits advisors) and upskilling of the existing workforce. The savings are only realized if these outcome shifts actually occur.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to assess delivery risk. Savings plans with outcome targets of this scale carry higher uncertainty than efficiency or contract cuts, and targets depend on successful service redesign and sustained performance.
findings.figures: £10,492,152 total savings over three years; £1,997,846 from accommodation options; £1,798,144 from improving practice; £458,874 from DWP benefits support; £799,896 from Care Undergraduate redesign
findings.quote: The current number of people living in their own home was 350 at 21/04/2026. This proposal linked with the other 2 proposals will see an increase of 30% in this cohort (105 people) and result in a reduction of care and support costs reflective of a less formal care environment.

findings.paper_title: 7g. Appendix 1 - Strategic Risk Register Sept 2026 v3
findings.headline: Forecast in-year overspend of £335k for 2026/27 despite corporate contingency use, driven by Children's, Adult Social Care, and Environment
findings.detail: The Q1 position shows a forecast overspend of £335k for the full year 2026/27. The main overspend areas are: Children's Services (cost of children in care and home-to-school transport); Adult Social Care (hospital discharge, increased eligible population, increased acuity); Environment (planning and bereavement income shortfalls). These are being partially offset by contingent resources set aside in the budget, but the register notes the forecast overspend is "now exceeding the council's in-year corporate contingency and the limited time in which to deliver additional mitigation."
findings.matters: A lender sees that despite contingency use and mitigation attempts, the council is still forecast to overspend in-year on demographic and demand pressures that show no sign of easing.
findings.figures: £335k forecast overspend; corporate contingency is circa £4m per annum
findings.quote: The council is projecting a materially balanced position (£335k forecast overspend) for 2026/27. The main forecast areas of overspending are Children's Services: including both the cost of supporting those children in the care of the authority, and home to school transport. Adult Social Care: High levels of hospital discharge, increases in the number of people eligible for support, and increases in the acuity of need.

findings.paper_title: 7g. Appendix 1 - Strategic Risk Register Sept 2026 v3
findings.headline: Waste contract risk improved from VERY HIGH to HIGH; interim two-year contract in place pending longer-term procurement
findings.detail: Risk 18 shows improvement from 25 VERY HIGH (December 2025) to 15 HIGH (current). The council has negotiated and mobilised a two-year interim contract with Veolia commencing 1 April 2026, providing continuity of statutory waste services after exit from the previous PPP contract. The council received a settlement sum from the previous contract. However, the register notes expected cost pressures from recyclate rebasing and the council must procure a longer-term solution by 1 April 2028.
findings.matters: A risk that threatened service failure has been mitigated with a stable interim contract, but the council must re-procure within two years and faces cost volatility from recycling markets.
findings.figures: Contract term: 1 April 2026 to 1 April 2028; score improved from 25 to 15
findings.quote: Risk score reduced this period due to the interim contract with Veolia but remains high as waste team procure a longer-term solution to 1 April 2028.

findings.paper_title: 7g. Appendix 1 - Strategic Risk Register Sept 2026 v3
findings.headline: Highways PFI contract risk substantially reduced from VERY HIGH to MEDIUM after resolving pricing disputes
findings.detail: Risk 20 shows significant improvement. The current score is 10 MEDIUM (down from 25 VERY HIGH in December 2025). The register notes: "differences in interpretation regarding pricing were resolved in July 2025 and both design and construction work is being commissioned and implemented." The reset action plan has worked and is now business as usual. NISTA funding for transformational change extended to March 2027. Two of three major workstreams complete.
findings.matters: A material operational and financial risk that has been a concern (assessed VERY HIGH only nine months ago) has been substantially mitigated. This is material good news for a lender: a council managing a very large PFI contract successfully through a dispute and reset is a positive signal of management capability during stress.
findings.figures: Score reduced from 25 (Dec 25) to 10 (Sep 26); 2/3 workstreams complete; NISTA funding to March 2027
findings.quote: Current score reduced to 10 MEDIUM, the differences in interpretation regarding pricing were resolved in July 2025 and both design and construction work is being commissioned and implemented.

findings.paper_title: 7g. Appendix 1 - Strategic Risk Register Sept 2026 v3
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer post vacant with significant recruitment challenges, creating instability in key statutory finance role
findings.detail: Risk 3 (Organisational Capacity) notes "There have been significant challenges in recruitment to the Director of Finance and s151 Officer post, leaving instability in a key senior role." The Section 151 Officer is the council's statutory financial officer and chief architect of its budget and financial strategy. An vacant post at this level is material instability at a time when the council is managing EFS and structural deficits of unprecedented scale.
findings.matters: A lender depends on stable financial leadership and the statutory officer's personal accountability for financial legality and proper accounting. A prolonged vacancy creates risk of continuity gaps, slower decision-making, and loss of institutional memory at a critical moment.
findings.figures: One director-level role unfilled; no timeline given for recruitment
findings.quote: There have been significant challenges in recruitment to the Director of Finance and s151 Officer post, leaving instability in a key senior role

findings.paper_title: 7g. Appendix 1 - Strategic Risk Register Sept 2026 v3
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support triggers External Assurance Review by Grant Thornton, with subsequent councils often receiving Best Value Notice
findings.detail: The council's receipt of EFS 'in principle' means it will be subject to an External Assurance Review undertaken by Grant Thornton on behalf of government. The risk register notes that "a number of authorities who have had EARs undertaken subsequently receive a Best Value Notice." A Best Value Notice is a formal government intervention measure. The risk register also notes that governance improvement activity remains at early stage and external auditor scrutiny is a significant factor in assessing effectiveness.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that the council is now subject to formal government oversight and faces material risk of a Best Value Notice, which is a statutory intervention that restricts council powers.
findings.figures: Grant Thornton undertaking EAR; governance improvement still early stage
findings.quote: Due to receiving "in principle" Exceptional Financial Support the council will be subject to an External Assurance Review (EAR) which will be undertaken by Grant Thornton on behalf of government - a number of authorities who have had EARs undertaken subsequently receive a Best Value Notice.

findings.paper_title: 7g. Appendix 1 - Strategic Risk Register Sept 2026 v3
findings.headline: Structural deficits forecast to grow to £40m in 2027/28 and £66m by 2029/30
findings.detail: The February 2026 Full Council instructed Directors to plan for a structural deficit of £40m for 2027/28, rising to £66m by 2029/30. An Improvement Board has been established to address this, with transformation plans to be incorporated into service business plans. These are projected figures, not current year actuals, but they represent the medium-term trajectory the council's leadership expects absent major service reductions or funding changes.
findings.matters: A lender seeing structural deficits of this scale three years out needs to understand whether the council has a funded or credible transformation plan to close them, and what service cuts or income changes this will require.
findings.quote: February Council instructed Directors to start planning how the Council will identify savings opportunities to contribute towards a Transformation Plan to address the forecast "Structural" Deficit of £40m for 2027/28, rising to £66m by 2029/30

findings.paper_title: 7g. Appendix 1 - Strategic Risk Register Sept 2026 v3
findings.headline: Council needed £12.9m government emergency loan to set a legal 2026/27 budget despite actual structural deficit of £20.4m
findings.detail: The council applied for and received Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) permission to borrow £12.9m to achieve a legally balanced position. The document states explicitly that without one-off resources, the underlying structural deficit is £20.4m. This is a deficit closed not by operational action but by emergency government lending, the only mechanism available to councils unable to balance a budget conventionally.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that the council cannot balance its budget without government emergency support, and that the underlying gap is 58% larger than the money borrowed to cover it.
findings.figures: £12.9m loan; £20.4m underlying structural deficit in 2026/27
findings.quote: Setting a legally balanced budget position for 2026/27 was only possible because the council applied for and received permission to drawdown a £12.9m loan. The underlying structural deficit in 2026/27 is £20.4m (it is only via the use of one-off resources that the amount has been reduced to £12.9m).

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: External audit opinions for 2024/25 and prior years were disclaimed due to limited audit timeframe in reset phase; full audit planned for 2025/26 accounts autumn 2026.
findings.detail: The council met the February 2026 backstop date for 2024/25 audit completion following national audit delays. However, auditors issued disclaimed opinions due to insufficient time to gather reliable evidence during the audit reset phase. A full audit is planned for autumn 2026 for the 2025/26 accounts to meet the January 2027 backstop date.
findings.matters: Disclaimed audit opinions remove external validation of financial statement reliability; lenders cannot rely on auditor assurance until full audits resume; auditor confidence deficit extends lender uncertainty about account quality.
findings.figures: February 2026 backstop date for 2024/25 audits met; disclaimed opinions issued; January 2027 backstop date for 2025/26; full audit planned autumn 2026
findings.quote: Like a significant proportion of local authorities, the limited timeframe for reset has meant auditors have not had sufficient time to gain enough reliable, appropriate evidence and have therefore issued disclaimed opinions on the accounts for recent years.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Pension Fund compliance with new Pension Act deadline of 30 June 2026 appears unlikely; fund may need to self-report to Pension Regulator.
findings.detail: A new Pension Act effective 30 June 2026 requires local government pension funds to join FCA-regulated investment pools. Although work continues for the Isle of Wight Pension Fund to join the Central investment pool, 'it looks increasing unlikely this will be feasible by 30 June 2026, meaning a self-report to the Pension Regulator will need to be considered.' Internal Audit identified three high-risk findings: action plan unrealistic expectations, inconsistent knowledge/understanding completion, and contributions reconciliation gaps.
findings.matters: Pension fund compliance failure and Pension Regulator self-report flag governance weakness affecting scheme members and attracting regulatory scrutiny; indicates capacity constraints preventing timely regulatory deadline compliance.
findings.figures: 30 June 2026 regulatory deadline; three high-risk audit findings on action plan pace, knowledge & understanding, and contributions reconciliation
findings.quote: At the time of writing, although work is continuing for the IWC pension Fund to join the Central investment pool, it looks increasing unlikely this will be feasible by 30 June 2026, meaning a self-report to the Pension Regulator will need to be considered.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Adult Social Care CQC assessment rated the service as 'requires improvement', though a separate Ofsted review of care leavers arrangements was positive.
findings.detail: The council received a CQC assessment of Adult Services rated as 'requires improvement'. This is noted in the context of broader organizational stress and increased whistle-blowing investigations. A separate Ofsted review of care leavers arrangements was positive, providing mixed signal on service quality.
findings.matters: Regulator concern about a major spending area (costs up £14.8m, 21% increase) signals service delivery and quality issues; regulators may impose intervention affecting operations or reputation; cost escalation and quality concerns compound financial risk.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care costs up £14.8m (21%); CQC rating 'requires improvement'; Ofsted care leavers review positive
findings.quote: the recent CQC assessment of Adult Services rated the service as 'requires improvement', although the Ofsted review of arrangements for care leavers earlier this year was positive.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Governance culture and constitutional compliance issues identified by statutory officers, including lack of respect for constitutional framework, potential Member-Officer Protocol breaches, and adversarial behaviours requiring external facilitated engagement.
findings.detail: Statutory officers raised concerns about organizational culture and governance. Key issues include lack of respect for the constitutional framework, potential breaches of the Member-Officer Protocol and Members Code of Conduct, adversarial behaviours, disregard for professional advice, and challenges to decision-making processes. The council has engaged senior councillors, developed a member development strategy and delivered an externally facilitated engagement programme to address these issues.
findings.matters: Governance culture failures compromise decision-making quality, undermine officer advice, create reputational risk, and indicate organizational dysfunction; they signal deeper control environment weakness beyond formal processes.
findings.figures: External facilitation required; new Standards Committee established but not yet meeting; comprehensive induction programme delivered
findings.quote: Key issues related to a lack of respect for the constitutional framework, including potential breaches of the Member-Officer Protocol, Members Code of Conduct, adversarial behaviours, lack of respect for professional advice and regular challenges to decision-making processes.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer and Director of Finance posts are being recruited following wind-down of strategic partnership with Portsmouth City Council; currently operating under interim arrangements.
findings.detail: The council previously obtained its Director of Finance, Section 151 Officer and Chief Internal Auditor roles through a strategic partnership with Portsmouth City Council. This arrangement is ending, and the council is recruiting its own finance leadership for 2026/27. Recruitment is underway but currently supported through interim arrangements.
findings.matters: Continuity and quality of senior finance leadership is critical to financial resilience; interim arrangements during a financial crisis period increase delivery risk; permanent recruitment may delay while council faces structural deficit.
findings.figures: S151 Officer and Director of Finance recruitment underway; interim arrangement in place; recruitment timeline to 2026/27
findings.quote: Recruitment is underway for the appointment of a dedicated S151 Officer and Director of Finance and for the Assistant Director of Finance. This is currently supported through an interim arrangement.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Waste contract contractor became financially unstable and the contract was terminated on 31 March 2026, requiring emergency management and new two-year interim procurement.
findings.detail: The waste contract risk reached a critical point due to the contractor's financial instability, forcing termination on 31 March 2026. The council managed the exit and secured waste service delivery for two years while undertaking a comprehensive procurement exercise for long-term arrangements, leaving the permanent solution uncertain.
findings.matters: Critical service delivery risk materialized and required emergency intervention; demonstrates vulnerability of large outsourced contracts and council's ability to manage contractor failure during a period of financial stress.
findings.figures: Waste contract termination 31 March 2026; two-year interim arrangement; service delivery secured pending procurement outcome
findings.quote: The waste contract risk reached a critical point due to the financial instability of the Council's waste contractor and the impending termination of that contract on 31 March 2026. This exit was effectively managed, and the delivery of waste services secured for the next two years.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Resource shortfalls have worsened materially in 2025/26 and are expected to continue through 2026/27, compromising the control environment during forced organizational change.
findings.detail: Internal Audit identified limited resources as a root cause of governance issues in 2024/25, and this has deteriorated. The statement notes 'both the shortfall in resources and the resulting impact having worsened during 2025/26; a trend which is likely to continue through 2026/27.' As a condition of exceptional funding, the council must prepare a transformation plan requiring significant change, placing further strain on already reduced capacity.
findings.matters: Resource constraints during mandatory recovery reduce capacity to execute change and maintain controls, increasing likelihood of service failures and control breakdowns; worsening capacity during financial crisis indicates loss of organizational resilience.
findings.figures: Resource shortfall identified, impact worsening from 2024/25 through 2025/26, trend expected to continue through 2026/27
findings.quote: In 2024/25 Internal Audit identified limited resources as a root cause of many issues. This continues to be the case but with both the shortfall in resources and the resulting impact having worsened during 2025/26; a trend which is likely to continue through 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Internal Audit issued one 'no assurance' report and two 'limited assurance' ratings in 2025/26, with audit opinion risk of downgrade in 2026/27
findings.detail: 2025/26 saw the first 'no assurance' audit report and two 'limited assurance' ratings, departing from prior years' mostly 'assurance' or 'reasonable assurance' ratings. High-risk findings increased within 'reasonable assurance' audits. The overall annual opinion remains 'reasonable assurance', but Internal Audit notes 'the direction of travel indicates that there is a risk that that the audit opinion for 2026/2027 may not sustain this position.'
findings.matters: Deteriorating audit opinions signal weakening control environment and governance effectiveness; a downgrade from reasonable to limited or no assurance would indicate material governance failure affecting financial statement reliability.
findings.figures: One 'no assurance' report; two 'limited assurance' ratings; increased high-risk findings within reasonable assurance audits in single year
findings.quote: 2025/26 has seen a 'no assurance' report issued by Internal Audit, with a further two areas rated 'limited assurance'. Across audits rated 'reasonable assurance' the number of individual findings rated 'high risk' has also increased.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 with Addendum A
findings.headline: Council required exceptional financial support from government to set 2026/27 budget, with a structural deficit of £20m rising to £65m by 2029/30 if unaddressed.
findings.detail: The council was one of 37 authorities requiring Exceptional Financial Support in 2026/27, with government permission to borrow £12.9m for day-to-day operational expenditure. The underlying structural deficit stems from £14.8m escalation in Adult Social Care costs, £6.5m doubling of waste contract costs, and £13.8m reduction in government funding over three years. Without intervention, the deficit could reach £65m by 2029/30.
findings.matters: Government intervention to balance a budget indicates financial unsustainability and puts the council in dependency on exceptional support while developing a recovery plan; this signals fundamental affordability issues for lenders.
findings.figures: £12.9m borrowing approval for operational expenditure; £20m structural deficit 2026/27; potential £65m by 2029/30; Adult Social Care £14.8m (21% increase); waste contract £6.5m doubling; government funding reduction £13.8m over 3 years (16%)
findings.quote: The setting of the Isle of Wight Councils budget for 2026/27 was its most challenging for at least the last ten-year period. A legally balanced budget was only achievable through the direct support of government and through their Exceptional Finance Support (EFS) programme

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Report - Reserve Risk Assessment Update
findings.headline: Four major reserves—General Fund, Capital Grants Unapplied, Revaluation Reserve, and Capital Adjustment Account—carry unaudited brought-forward balances from 2023/24 and 2024/25.
findings.detail: These reserves carry opening balances from the disclaimed audit years that were never independently verified. Post-disclaimer audit procedures focused only on current-year movements, not underlying balances. The General Fund and Capital Adjustment Account are both described as material and highly complex.
findings.matters: Unaudited reserve balances mean the council's stated financial position and available resources lack independent verification for 2-3 years of cumulative transactions, materially undermining statement reliability.
findings.figures: Four reserves affected; balances at 31 March 2023 and 2024 unaudited
findings.quote: Whilst audit procedures in subsequent years have provided assurance over movements in the General Fund, the closing balances at 31 March 2023 and 31 March 2024 were not audited due to the disclaimer of opinion. Consequently, assurance has not been obtained over the underlying brought-forward balances.

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Report - Reserve Risk Assessment Update
findings.headline: Audit fees will vary beyond the standard scale fee due to additional work on reserve rebuild and historical assurance procedures.
findings.detail: EY explicitly states that activities relating to the reserve risk assessment and rebuilding of historical assurance are outside the scale fee. The auditor is seeking a formal variation to the scale fee, indicating material additional costs beyond the baseline audit contract.
findings.matters: Rising audit costs reflect the council's need for more intensive work due to control and documentation gaps, adding financial pressure.
findings.figures: Variation amount TBD; services outside April 2026 planning scope
findings.quote: procedures relating to the rebuilding of historical assurance will also be outside the scale fee. Accordingly, we will seek a variation to the scale fee to reflect these changes to the scope of our work

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Report - Reserve Risk Assessment Update
findings.headline: Two unresolved accounting issues identified in 2024/25—waste asset valuation and school IFRS 16 treatment—remain to be addressed in 2025/26.
findings.detail: EY identified a waste asset valuation matter affecting the revaluation reserve and a schools IFRS 16 consideration affecting the capital adjustment account. Both issues are expected to be resolved in 2025/26. These represent known accounting uncertainties that originated in the disclaimed years and have carried forward.
findings.matters: Known unresolved accounting issues indicate control and documentation weaknesses that affect financial reporting reliability.
findings.figures: Two matters identified 2024/25; resolution expected 2025/26
findings.quote: In 24/25, a specific outstanding matter relating to waste asset valuation was identified, which may impact the revaluation reserve. In 2024–25, a specific matter relating to the consideration of schools under IFRS 16 has been identified, which may impact the Capital Adjustment Account.

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Report - Reserve Risk Assessment Update
findings.headline: The council's path to an unqualified audit opinion extends to at least 2029/30 or beyond, constrained by a 5-year property revaluation cycle.
findings.detail: EY notes that properties last valued in the disclaimed years 2022/23 and 2023/24 will not be revalued until 2027/28 and 2028/29. The auditor states it cannot move forward from a qualified (except for) opinion until this revaluation cycle is completed, meaning unqualified status is not achievable until after that work is done.
findings.matters: Extended periods of qualified or disclaimed opinions restrict the council's access to capital markets and increase borrowing costs, as lenders price in elevated risk.
findings.figures: 5-year valuation cycle; next revaluation due 2027/28-2028/29
findings.quote: The Council has a 5 year rolling programme and properties last valued in 2022/23 and 2023/24, both disclaimed, would next be valued in 2027/28 and 2028/29. Therefore, we may not be able to move forward from a qualified (except for) opinion until this cycle is completed.

findings.paper_title: 6a. External Auditors Report - Reserve Risk Assessment Update

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 4 - Responses to Audit and Governance Committee questions from July 2026 committee (1)
findings.headline: Council acknowledges it cannot systematically publish required contract details notices due to resource constraints.

The council stated this will be reviewed in future.
findings.matters: A council that acknowledges being unable to meet contract transparency requirements due to resource constraints signals both a control gap and resourcing issue that lenders assess when evaluating governance quality and management capacity.

findings.headline: Procurement team is understaffed with ongoing resource gaps affecting its ability to deliver oversight in timely manner.
findings.detail: The team is described as 'relatively small' with 'ongoing resourcing gaps' despite responsibility for contracts over £30,000 (inc. VAT) across all directorates. The report notes that 'capacity demands impact ability to deliver all procurement related projects in timely manner.'
findings.matters: Procurement oversight is a key financial control; an understaffed team risks failures in compliance monitoring, spending scrutiny, and contract management.
findings.figures: No staff numbers disclosed; team responsible for contracts over £30,000 inc. VAT
findings.quote: The team is relatively small in size and has responsibility for delivering a wide range of statutory, governance and operational procurement functions, which is further compounded by ongoing resourcing gaps within the team.

findings.headline: Council has identified significant gaps in its procurement data collection that prevent reliable comparison to historical records.
findings.detail: Officers reviewed how procurement data was captured and found inconsistencies and gaps requiring remediation. The contract register shows £1.20bn in contracts, but some entries lack stated values; the council states 'the actual figures are likely to be higher than shown above.' Direct comparison to prior years cannot be assured due to these historical gaps.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence the council can accurately track and report on financial commitments; data quality gaps in procurement suggest control weaknesses that could mask other financial risks.

findings.quote: As a consequence of these changes, together with inconsistencies and gaps identified in the previous processes, direct comparison with historic data cannot be fully assured.

findings.headline: CMT has identified a new strategic risk that significant government policy changes will outpace the council's organisational readiness, risking statutory non-compliance, unfunded mandates and financial pressures.
findings.detail: The council's Corporate Management Team has added a new strategic risk to the register relating to government policy changes including the Families First Programme, Social Work Reform, NHS 10-Year Plan, Local Government Reorganisation, Devolution settlements, and Planning & Infrastructure Act. The risk is that policy changes will introduce statutory duties, funding conditions, structural changes, and reporting requirements faster than the council can implement them. Consequences explicitly identified by the council include financial pressures (overspends, cost of compliance, stranded costs during reorganisation), disruption to critical children's, adults, health and care services, legal challenges, workforce turnover, partnership breakdown, and capital programme delays.
findings.matters: A lender would care because unfunded mandates, statutory non-compliance, and financial pressures from unplanned policy changes could significantly impact the council's financial position, service delivery capability, and creditworthiness.

findings.quote: CMT have identified the risk that significant changes from new or amended government policy will outpace organisational readiness, leading to statutory non‑compliance, unfunded mandates, disruption to critical services (children's, adults, health & care, planning, and infrastructure), workforce shortages, partnership fragmentation, and reputational harm.

findings.headline: Multiple system access control and security patching weaknesses in network infrastructure
findings.detail: The Local Network audit identified several control weaknesses: 36 staff hold administrative system access (higher than normally expected, though work is underway to restrict this); 10 of 38 Linux servers run unsupported versions; 4 of 156 Windows servers have unconfirmed patching status. findings.matters: Weak access controls and outdated or unpatched systems create cybersecurity and operational resilience risks that could compromise the council's ability to deliver services and protect sensitive data—material concerns for any lender evaluating operational stability.

While primarily based on MS Windows a small number of servers (38) are running versions of Linux. Of these a subset of ten are running out of support versions which, where possible, need to be updated.

findings.matters: Failure to follow procurement procedures creates risk of overpaying, eliminates competitive tension in purchasing, and prevents effective budget management—a fundamental financial control concern for any lender or finance director.

The Code now prohibits councils from borrowing to invest primarily for financial return. The council explicitly states it will review options for exiting these investments before undertaking further borrowing, creating a hard constraint on capital funding capacity.
findings.matters: This restriction limits the council's ability to borrow for capital projects unless or until these investments are divested, reducing financial flexibility precisely when councils are evaluating spending on infrastructure and services.

Affordable housing (£36.9m) and regeneration (£4.0m) are not yet approved pending business case sign-off. If these cases do not proceed, the capital programme will require material repricing.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to know whether the capital programme depends on approvals that may not materialise, and what the contingency plan is if they fail.

The council acknowledges timing risk between expenditure incurrence and cash realisation from asset sales. Government is also directing the council to maximise capital receipts to avoid EFS borrowing.
findings.matters: Capital receipts shortfall could force unplanned borrowing if timings slip; government is explicitly expecting capital receipts to minimise EFS reliance, creating additional pressure.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £17.1m creates £5.4m residual council liability when statutory override ends March 2028
findings.detail: The council has an accumulated DSG deficit of £17.1m as of 31 March 2026 (would have been £26.8m but for £9.6m prior government support). A statutory override allows this to be held in unusable reserves until 31 March 2028. Government is providing 90% support toward DSG deficits, but the council will face a residual liability of £5.4m when the override ends. Provision has been made in the Financial Sustainability Earmarked Reserve.
findings.matters: DSG deficit creates a 2028 cliff edge when the statutory override ends; the £5.4m residual liability compounds the structural deficit at that point.

findings.detail: Ten maintained primary schools are forecasting cumulative deficits of £1.8m by March 2028 (based on May 2026 budget submissions). Declining pupil rolls create inefficiency and unbalanced budgets. The council has no power to write off individual school deficits but becomes liable for balance sheet deficits when a school closes, creating potential future crystallisation of liabilities.
findings.matters: School deficits compound the council's structural deficit and create a 2028 cliff edge when statutory overrides end; potential school closures could trigger asset write-offs.
findings.figures: £1.8m forecast deficit across 10 primary schools by March 2028; 10 of 31 maintained primary schools affected

findings.headline: Waste contract procurement risk remains material; current Veolia contract cost-plus through 2028/29 only
findings.detail: The council's long-term waste provider exited in 2025/26, causing immediate cost doubling. A two-year cost-plus contract with Veolia was placed, adding £6.5m in 2026/27 and £9m from 2027/28. Long-term procurement is underway, but final contract certainty is absent until concluded. Waste is the second-largest driver of the identified structural deficit.
findings.matters: Waste is material to the £66m structural deficit; procurement risk is live as current contract is time-limited and cost-plus; failure to secure lower-cost long-term provision will worsen deficit trajectory.
findings.figures: £6.5m additional cost 2026/27; £9m from 2027/28; waste is £6.5m of the structural deficit

findings.headline: External assurance review by CIPFA and Grant Thornton commenced August 2026 to assess financial position and governance
findings.detail: As a condition of exceptional financial support, government commissioned an external assurance review to assess the council's financial position and governance. CIPFA leads the financial assessment, with Grant Thornton and Peopletoo in partnership. The review began August 2026. Although a Best Value Notice is not certain, some authorities with prolonged EFS reliance have received one, signalling formal government expectations for improvement.
findings.matters: External scrutiny provides independent validation of position and potential lever for improvement; a Best Value Notice would signal formal escalation and additional oversight for lenders.

findings.headline: Quarter 1 2026/27 shows structural deficit pressures materialising with £335k forecast deficit despite contingency deployment
findings.detail: Q1 budget monitoring shows the council forecasting a £335k deficit despite the balanced budget framework and contingency deployment. Emerging pressures are: children's services placements and transport costs, adult social care hospital discharge activity and acuity increases, and planning and bereavement services income shortfalls. Savings delivery is tracking at 84% plan, with £557k shortfall forecast. Services have deployed mitigations and contingencies are being drawn to offset pressures.
findings.matters: Early visibility of demand pressures shows the structural deficit is a current operational reality, not just a medium-term forecast; early contingency deployment limits flexibility later in the year.

findings.headline: £6.738m of earmarked reserves released with Section 151 Officer satisfied remaining reserves are adequate for risk mitigation
findings.detail: The council released £6.738m from earmarked reserves: £714k from the highways PFI pension liability reserve (low risk; no contributions required until 2029), £4.371m from accumulated risk contingency not previously used, and £1.653m from the capital resources reserve. The Section 151 Officer confirmed the remaining reserves are adequate for the risks they mitigate, with benchmarking showing above-average useable reserves relative to core spending power.
findings.matters: Reserve release improves current-year liquidity; S151 Officer assurance on adequacy is material given the council is under external assurance review and faces medium-term structural deficit.

findings.headline: Capital programme reset removes £19.164m of assumed future prudential borrowing and continues reduction in Capital Financing Requirement
findings.detail: The council conducted a fundamental reset of its capital programme, removing legacy, stalled, and inactive schemes and reprofiling housing investment. This action removed £19.164m of assumed future prudential borrowing and released £57k of revenue resources. The council's CFR stands at £377m—higher than average compared to peer authorities—but has been reducing faster than peers.
findings.matters: Material reduction in assumed future borrowing improves the debt trajectory and sustainability; CFR reduction also frees revenue capacity as capital financing requirements diminish.

findings.headline: 2025/26 financial outturn delivered £4.798m underspend despite £10.4m corporate contingency for exceptional service pressures
findings.detail: The council's approved 2025/26 budget of £214.2m included a £10.4m contingency to cover exceptional cost pressures in adult and children's services. Despite this, the council delivered an overall saving of £4.798m (2.2%). This underspend was transferred to a Financial Sustainability Earmarked Reserve and was material in eliminating the need for EFS borrowing in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A council delivering under budget in a year of exceptional pressures demonstrates operational control and provides evidence that services can manage within budget envelopes; the outturn improves confidence in the 2026/27 forecast.

findings.headline: Structural deficit forecast at £66.3m by 2029/30 with no quantified solution identified, driven by adult social care, waste costs, and funding cuts
findings.detail: The council's day-to-day operational expenditure is forecast to exceed operational income by £66.3m by 2029/30 (28% of net budget), up from £12.9m in 2026/27. Drivers are: adult social care escalation (£14.8m), waste contract doubling (£6.5m rising to £9m), and government funding reductions (£3.1m per annum rising to £13.1m over three years). Interest alone on EFS borrowing to fund this would cost £17.5m annually. The response centres on establishing an improvement board and directing services to find savings, but no specific plan to close the deficit is presented.
findings.matters: A structural deficit of this scale represents an existential threat to financial sustainability; for peer councils, it illustrates the cumulative pressure from demand, government funding policy, and commercial contracts; lenders assess whether transformation activity can realistically bridge it.
findings.figures: £66.3m structural deficit by 2029/30; £14.8m adult social care; £6.5m–£9m waste; £3.1m–£13.1m government funding cuts; £17.5m annual EFS interest

findings.headline: 2026/27 exceptional financial support borrowing requirement eliminated to zero through capital reset, reserve release, and underspend deployment
findings.detail: The council had government approval for £12.881m in exceptional financial support (EFS) borrowing for 2026/27 to balance its budget. Through application of a £4.798m underspend from 2025/26, release of £6.738m earmarked reserves, capital programme reset generating £57k revenue, and release of £1.288m budgeted EFS debt costs, the council has reduced the 2026/27 EFS requirement to nil, subject to services managing within approved budgets and contingencies.
findings.matters: A council with government support but taking concrete action to eliminate the immediate borrowing need demonstrates operational control and financial discipline; also materially improves the in-year revenue position for 2026/27.
findings.figures: £12.881m original EFS approval; £4.798m underspend; £6.738m reserves; £57k capital; £1.288m EFS provision; £0m forecast borrowing

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Proposed Land and Property Asset Disposal Policy
findings.headline: Asset disposals are being used to generate capital receipts for the Medium-Term Financial Plan
findings.detail: The policy states that disposal of land and property assets will 'help generate capital receipts to support the Council's Medium-Term Financial Plan'. The council has established a six-monthly review cycle to identify surplus assets for disposal, indicating a systematic approach to generating these receipts as part of the capital funding strategy.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's capital programme is dependent on asset sales, and whether the SRH housing constraint or the governance changes might affect the council's ability to dispose of assets as planned.
findings.figures: Six-monthly asset review cycle
findings.quote: Where appropriate, the disposal of land and property assets will help generate capital receipts to support the Council's Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP) and deliver key outcomes from the Corporate Plan.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Proposed Land and Property Asset Disposal Policy
findings.headline: Asset disposal decision authority has shifted from Full Council to the Policy, Finance and Resources Committee under governance amendments finalised August 2026
findings.detail: The governance structure governing asset disposals has been materially changed. Previously Full Council made all decisions on asset categories and disposals; the current policy (draft 1.2, August 2026) gives the PFRC authority to determine asset categories and decide whether to proceed with disposals, with Full Council involvement now limited to matters of exceptional strategic significance. These changes reflect the Constitutional Position determined by Annual Council on 27 May 2026.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender would need to know that the governance of asset sales—a key source of capital receipts—has been changed to centre on committee rather than full council decision-making, potentially affecting decision speed and oversight.
findings.figures: Annual Council decision 27 May 2026; amendments finalised 16 August 2026
findings.quote: Responsibility for land and property matters rests with the Policy, Finance and Resources Committee except where the Constitution provides otherwise or where the Policy, Finance and Resources Committee determines that referral to Full Council is appropriate.

findings.paper_title: 7c. Appendix 1 - Proposed Land and Property Asset Disposal Policy
findings.headline: Full Council resolution requires all asset disposals to be assessed for social rent housing potential first, before other uses
findings.detail: From 15 January 2025, any Council-owned land or buildings being considered for sale or development must first be assessed for their potential to provide social rent housing. This assessment applies to all disposals and is the first test before assets can be declared suitable for other purposes. The policy establishes a mandatory viability assessment based on economic, social and environmental criteria.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to understand if this housing-first constraint limits which assets can be sold and at what price, affecting capital receipt projections in the Medium-Term Financial Plan.
findings.figures: Resolution passed 15 January 2025; policy approved Full Council 16 July 2025
findings.quote: Full Council passed a resolution on 15 January 2025 requiring that any Council-owned land or buildings being considered for sale or development must first be assessed for their potential to provide SRH.

findings.headline: Chief Finance Officer advises council not to consider any new discretionary policy initiatives that would increase expenditure while under Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer explicitly recommends against committing to any new discretionary spending while reliant on EFS. The paper notes that even a 5 per cent increase in LCTS support would cost approximately £370,000 annually. This constraint is binding policy choices: the committee is being asked not to consult on potential improvements to the welfare scheme, not because consultation is undesirable in principle, but because "there is presently no financially viable scheme for consultation".
findings.matters: This is a formal control mechanism signaling that a council's policy flexibility is constrained by financial distress; it shows how EFS operates in practice and how a council under structural deficit cannot easily commit to new spending.
findings.figures: £370,000 annual cost for a 5 per cent increase in LCTS support
findings.quote: the council's Section 151 Officer advises that the Council should not consider any new policy initiative at this time that would increase the financial burden upon the Council

findings.headline: Council facing £13.8 million reduction in revenue support grant over 2026/27 to 2028/29, with LCTS funding merged into grant and arguably no longer funded
findings.detail: LCTS funding was merged into the general revenue support grant in 2013. The paper states that reductions in this funding since 2021, combined with the £13.8 million reduction IWC faces over the next three years, make it "arguable as to whether the Council receives any government support for its ongoing LCTS scheme". This suggests the council may be funding the welfare scheme entirely from its own resources while the structural deficit grows.
findings.matters: Loss of identifiable funding for welfare support indicates that a council under structural deficit is prioritizing welfare spending from general funds, narrowing the scope for other service investment or deficit reduction.
findings.figures: £13.8 million revenue support grant reduction over 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.quote: Reductions in this funding since 2021 and the £13.8m reduction the Council faces over the next three years (2026/26 to 2028/29) make it arguable as to whether the Council receives any government support for its ongoing LCTS scheme.

findings.headline: Collection rate from working-age LCTS claimants at 82.86 per cent in 2025/26, against 95 per cent overall, with £2.95 million retrospective debt outstanding since 2013
findings.detail: The council's overall Council Tax collection rate is stable at around 95 per cent, but working-age LCTS claimants collect at only 82.86 per cent (ranging 80.67–82.86 per cent from 2021/22 to 2025/26). Retrospective LCTS debt stretches back to 2013 and totals £2.95 million as of March 2026. About 25 per cent of single claimants hold at least one unpaid liability order—11 percentage points above the average across all LCTS claimants.
findings.matters: This indicates financial stress among the poorest residents and represents direct income risk to the council; it also signals that welfare spending may not reach those most in need if collection is poor, and for a council already in structural deficit, any further income loss is material.
findings.figures: Working-age collection 82.86% (2025/26) versus 95% overall; £2.95 million retrospective debt; 25% of single claimants with unpaid liability orders
findings.quote: Whilst the overall level of Council Tax 'in-year' collection on the Isle of Wight has remained relatively stable at around 95 per cent over recent years, collection levels from working-age LCTS claimants is much lower: 82.86 per cent

findings.headline: Local Council Tax Support scheme cost increased from £10.04 million to £11.20 million despite claimant numbers falling from 10,741 to 9,330 between 2018/19 and 2025/26
findings.detail: Although the number of people claiming support has declined steadily, the total cost of the scheme has risen. The paper identifies Council Tax increases as the driver: as the council raises its tax bills (partly to finance other services), claimants automatically receive higher support amounts to maintain the same proportion of cover. The paper warns that if Council Tax continues to increase, scheme costs will continue rising despite stable or declining caseload.
findings.matters: This reveals a fiscal feedback loop: raising Council Tax to fund services or service debt worsens the welfare bill, compounding financial pressure on a council already running a structural deficit.
findings.quote: It can be seen from the above tables that the total number of claimants has slowly decreased since 2018, however the cost of the scheme since 2018/19 has been rising.

findings.headline: Structural budget deficit forecast to reach £66.3 million annually by 2029/30, funded by £175.3 million borrowing over four years through Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: The council's structural deficit—the gap between income and expenditure—is £12.9 million in 2026/27 and is forecast to rise to £66.3 million by 2029/30. Under Exceptional Financial Support, the council is permitted to borrow to cover day-to-day revenue expenditure (normally prohibited) and must repay over 20 years with interest. The deficit is widening partly because the borrowing itself creates capital and interest repayment costs.
findings.matters: A council with a structural deficit cannot easily adapt to shocks and has constrained policy flexibility; the widening deficit and debt service obligations are material to any lender assessing sustainability.
findings.figures: £12.9 million structural deficit in 2026/27; £66.3 million by 2029/30; £175.3 million total borrowing 2026/27 to 2029/30
findings.quote: The February 2026 approved budget set out that this borrowing is designed to address the Council's underlying gap between its income and expenditure (structural deficit) which is estimated to amount to £12.9 million in 2026/27 and is forecast to increase to £66.3 million annually by 2029/30

findings.headline: Isle of Wight requires Exceptional Financial Support from central government, constraining discretionary policy decisions
findings.detail: The Council is facing its most significant financial challenge in at least a decade. The Section 151 Officer has advised that no new discretionary policy initiatives should be undertaken if they would increase the council's financial burden while it requires Exceptional Financial Support from central government. The LCTS scheme for 2027/28 will therefore remain unchanged with no public consultation.
findings.matters: Exceptional Financial Support is a formal intervention signal indicating severe financial stress; lenders assess this when evaluating council creditworthiness, and peer finance directors track how it constrains operational decisions.
findings.figures: Most significant financial challenge in at least a decade
findings.quote: the Council's Section 151 Officer has advised that consideration should not be given to any new discretionary policy initiatives that would increase the financial burden on the Council – particularly whilst it requires Exceptional Financial Support from central government

findings.headline: Council approved £4.287m savings and income generation for 2026/27, with £3.5m in-year delivery
findings.detail: The council approved £4.287m of savings, efficiencies and additional income generation on 25 February 2026 as part of setting the 2026/27 budget. Of this total, £3.5m is based on proposals with in-year effect deliverable in 2026/27. These demonstrate active deficit management, though they address less than a quarter of the £20m structural deficit.
findings.matters: A lender needs evidence that the council is actively delivering savings and managing the deficit, not relying solely on government support.
findings.figures: Approved savings £4.287m; in-year delivery £3.5m
findings.quote: Implementation of the actions required to deliver the £4.287m of savings, efficiencies and additional income generation agreed by Council on the 25 February 2026 in setting the 2026/27 Budget. Some of these individual proposals were based on a part year effect with £3.5m of the total assume d as deliverable in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Transformation Fund holds £9.5m uncommitted (July 2026) with intent to add £1m per annum
findings.detail: The council has established a Transformation Fund as an Earmarked Reserve with £9.5m available and uncommitted as of July 2026. The council intends to top this up by £1m per annum to support the ongoing reduction of cost base and improvement of operating efficiency. Allocations are made based on robust business cases demonstrating deliverable savings.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether the council's transformation investment is sufficient to deliver the scale of savings needed to close the structural deficit.
findings.figures: Transformation Fund £9.5m uncommitted (July 2026); planned annual top-up £1m per annum
findings.quote: As of July 2026, there was approximately £9.5m in the Transformation Fund available and uncommitted. The current intent is to top up these resources by £1m per annum in recognition of the ongoing need to reduce the cost base of the council and improve its operating efficiency.

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget only met legal requirement once EFS facility incorporated, despite being prepared with resilience
findings.detail: The council describes the 2026/27 budget setting as the most challenging in the past 10 years. The budget could only be considered legal once it incorporated the EFS facility, which is a standby debt facility incurred only if drawn upon. This demonstrates the severity of the budget challenge.
findings.matters: A lender would view dependence on an emergency facility to pass a legal budget as a significant concern about the council's underlying financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Most challenging budget setting in past 10 years
findings.quote: The Budget for 2026/27, prepared responsibly and with sufficient resilience, was only considered to be a legal Budget once it incorporated a debt facility (which is only incurred if drawn upon) provided by Central Government and known as Exceptional Financial Support (EFS).

findings.headline: DSG deficit of £27.1m at March 2026, with £4.6m residual liability emerging when statutory override expires March 2028, not yet in MTFS forecasts
findings.detail: The council has a DSG deficit of £27.1m at March 2026, with further deficits of £18.8m expected to accumulate until March 2028. A statutory override currently prevents these deficits needing to be overtly funded. The government will take over SEND funding from 1 April 2028 and will fund 90% of DSG deficits, leaving a residual liability of £4.6m to fall to the council once the override ends. Crucially, this £4.6m liability has not yet been factored into the MTFS forecasts.
findings.matters: A lender needs to identify emerging liabilities not yet reflected in council forecasts and understand when the council will need to address the £4.6m gap.
findings.figures: DSG deficit March 2026: £27.1m; further accumulated deficits to March 2028: £18.8m; residual liability from March 2028: £4.6m; government funds 90% of DSG deficits
findings.quote: From those statements, it is expected that 90% of all DSG deficits that arise will be funded by central Government, leaving a residual liability that is estimated to fall to the Council once the statutory override comes to an end in March 2028 of £4.6m

findings.headline: Council received 2.5% funding increase against 5.7% national average in 2026/27, creating structural imbalance
findings.detail: Isle of Wight's funding increase in 2026/27 was just 2.5%, compared to the 5.7% national average intended to cover inflation and rising demand. This disparity prevents the council from matching cost growth with income growth, and is directly cited as a source of the structural imbalance.
findings.matters: Finance directors need to distinguish between sector-wide pressures and particular disadvantage, and may use this as evidence in lobbying for funding adjustment.
findings.figures: Isle of Wight funding increase 2.5%; national average funding increase 5.7%
findings.quote: At the national level, funding for Local Government was expected to increase by 5.7% in 2026/27 to cover both inflation and rising demand. In contrast, the funding increase for the Isle of Wight Council was just 2.5% using the Government's measure.

findings.headline: Council forecasts £20m structural deficit for 2026/27, potentially rising to £66m by 2029/30, with forecast EFS drawdowns totaling £175.3m
findings.detail: Isle of Wight faces an underlying structural deficit of almost £20m for 2026/27, which could rise to £66m by 2029/30 without intervention. The council is in the Exceptional Financial Support programme and forecasts cumulative EFS drawdowns of £12.9m (2026/27), £39.7m (2027/28), £56.4m (2028/29), and £66.3m (2029/30). The accumulated EFS debt is forecast at £17.5m per annum by 2029/30.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the trajectory of the council's debt burden and whether it has a credible plan to exit EFS and manage this accumulating debt.
findings.figures: Structural deficit £20m (2026/27); £66m by 2029/30 if unaddressed; EFS drawdowns £12.9m, £39.7m, £56.4m, £66.3m, total £175.3m; accumulated debt £17.5m per annum by 2029/30
findings.quote: The scale of the Budget challenge for 2026/27 was considerable with an underlying "Structural" Deficit of almost £20m which if left unattended could rise to £66m by 2029/30 as set out in the table below.

findings.paper_title: 7f. Workforce Capacity, Structure and Delivery of Financial Sustainability
findings.headline: Council faces structural budget deficit projected to increase over medium term if not addressed
findings.detail: The council faces a significant and sustained financial challenge characterized by a structural budget deficit that is projected to increase over the medium term without corrective action. This is not a short-term challenge and requires strategic action to secure longer-term financial sustainability.
findings.matters: A structural deficit projected to worsen is a key financial risk signal for lenders assessing the council's financial trajectory and medium-term resilience.
findings.figures: Deficit size not quantified in this paper
findings.quote: The Council faces a significant and sustained financial challenge with a structural budget deficit that is projected to increase over the medium term if not addressed.

findings.paper_title: 7f. Workforce Capacity, Structure and Delivery of Financial Sustainability
findings.headline: Council already facing capacity pressures; workforce reductions risk compromising service delivery and statutory responsibilities if not carefully aligned
findings.detail: The council's strategic risk register already identifies ongoing risks relating to organisational capacity and resilience. The report notes the council is not starting from a position of excess capacity and emphasizes that workforce reductions not aligned to service priorities and future operating model could compromise the council's ability to deliver key services and discharge statutory responsibilities.
findings.matters: Where a council must achieve workforce savings for financial sustainability but already faces documented capacity constraints and audit concerns about limited resources, the operational risk to service delivery and further audit findings materially increases.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Within that context it is also important to recognise that capacity pressures already exist across services. These pressures are reflected within the Council's strategic risk register which identifies ongoing risks relating to organisational capacity, resilience and the ability to sustainably deliver priorities

findings.paper_title: 7f. Workforce Capacity, Structure and Delivery of Financial Sustainability
findings.headline: Internal audit identifies limited resources as recurring root cause of control weakness; council operating under considerable organisational stress
findings.detail: The council's most recent internal audit annual opinion identifies limited resources as a recurring root cause of weakness across service areas. The audit notes that the council is operating under considerable organisational stress, and that transformation and recovery activity will place additional pressures on the control environment and operational resilience.
findings.matters: Audit findings on organizational capacity and control environment are a key indicator of financial and operational risk material to creditworthiness assessment and peer council monitoring.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: It notes that the Council is operating under considerable organisational stress and that the transformation and recovery activity will place additional pressures on the organisations control environment and operational resilience.

findings.paper_title: 7f. Workforce Capacity, Structure and Delivery of Financial Sustainability
findings.headline: Council committed to £1.181m staff cost reduction programme, with £541k targeted for delivery in 2026/27
findings.detail: In February 2026, the council agreed a £1.181m staff cost reduction programme as part of its response to a structural budget deficit. £541k of this reduction is expected to be delivered in 2026/27 through workforce changes, without requiring compulsory redundancies. The council is implementing the Mutually Agreed Resignation Scheme (MARS) as an additional mechanism to support delivery of these savings.
findings.matters: Lenders and peer finance directors need to understand how a council with a structural deficit is executing specific financial recovery actions and the mechanisms being used to deliver them.
findings.figures: £1.181m total staff cost reduction; £541k in 2026/27
findings.quote: In setting the 2026/27 Budget in February 2026 Council agreed the implementation of a £1.181m staff cost reduction programme of which £541k was assumed for delivery in 2026/27(without the need for compulsory redundancies).

findings.paper_title: 7a. Appendix 3 - Proposed Removal from Capital Programme
findings.headline: East Cowes Landslip project abandoned with no spend recorded since 2023 and no planned spend
findings.detail: A £13.9k capital receipt project is being removed with the explicit reason "No spend since 2023, no planned spend". This represents programme abandonment or indefinite postponement of a scheme expected to have begun by now.
findings.matters: Long-dormant capital projects indicate either misjudged priorities or barriers to delivery that lenders need to understand.
findings.quote: No spend since 2023, no planned spend

findings.paper_title: 7a. Appendix 3 - Proposed Removal from Capital Programme
findings.headline: Decarbonisation (Salix) projects affected by contractor no longer running, retention payments from March 2024 unresolved
findings.detail: Two decarbonisation projects at Medina Leisure (£12.5k) and Heights (£8.2k) are being removed. The reasoning given is "Retention payments from March 24 - Company no longer running", indicating the contractor has ceased operations while retention amounts from an earlier phase remain outstanding.
findings.matters: Contractor failure during capital projects creates delivery risk and potential financial exposure; of concern to councils planning decarbonisation programmes.
findings.figures: £12,470 (Medina Leisure), £8,247 (Heights)
findings.quote: Retention payments from March 24 - Company no longer running

findings.paper_title: 7a. Appendix 3 - Proposed Removal from Capital Programme
findings.headline: Match funding from Environment Agency no longer required for £1.47m coastal protection scheme
findings.detail: The EA scheme Ventnor coastal protection project (£1.47m borrowing) is being removed because "Match funding for EA Schemes no longer required". This represents withdrawal or postponement of external funding that the council was relying on.
findings.matters: Councils dependent on external co-funding face delivery risk when partners withdraw; lenders need visibility of this funding dependency.
findings.quote: Match funding for EA Schemes no longer required

findings.paper_title: 7a. Appendix 3 - Proposed Removal from Capital Programme
findings.headline: Four major 2027-28 capital projects totalling £17.6m removed due to lack of plans
findings.detail: Regeneration funding (£2.11m), Medina valley KMP (£500k), VQ Other next phase (£10m), and Newport Harbour (£5m) are all listed for removal. Each is cited with the same reasoning: "Subject to business case - No plans". Together they represent most of the £19.2m borrowing being removed from the 2027-28 budget.
findings.matters: Capital programme flexibility and readiness affect the council's medium-term borrowing strategy and delivery capability, both of which lenders and peer councils monitor.
findings.figures: £2,110,381 (Regeneration), £500,000 (Medina valley), £10,000,000 (VQ Other), £5,000,000 (Newport Harbour); total borrowing removed 2027-28: £19,164,251
findings.quote: Subject to business case - No plans

findings.headline: Council rebuilding General Fund Reserve to minimise potential drawdown of Exceptional Financial Support in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council is transferring a £4.798m underspend (2.2% of gross budget) to the General Fund Reserve. The stated purpose is to 'provide greater resilience in 2026/27 in order to minimise the potential drawdown of Exceptional Financial Support'. This signals that the council is managing vulnerability to requiring emergency government financial support and is rebuilding reserves to reduce reliance on it.
findings.matters: The need to manage exposure to Exceptional Financial Support is an indicator of financial pressures and would be closely monitored by lenders and peer councils assessing financial health.
findings.figures: £4.798m underspend transferred to General Fund Reserve
findings.quote: To replenish the reserve to provide greater resilience in 2026/27 in order to minimise the potential drawdown of Exceptional Financial Support

findings.headline: Children's Services overspent by £2.817m, driven by residential care placements and agency staffing costs
findings.detail: Children's Services is forecast to overspend by £2.817m on a budget of £41.973m, reaching £44.790m outturn. The main pressures are in residential care placements and agency staffing, only partially offset by savings elsewhere in the service. This compounds the council's wider social care pressures.
findings.matters: Children's looked-after care pressures, particularly in residential placements and agency staffing, are a persistent challenge for councils and signal demand and capacity constraints that affect medium-term financial planning.
findings.figures: Budget £41.973m, forecast outturn £44.790m, overspend £2.817m
