findings.quote: Pressure in residential care placements and agency staff offset in part by Next Steps Support costs, fostering, Special Guardianship Orders, agency domiciliary costs and secure remand costs

findings.headline: Adult Social Care care packages overspent by £11.684m despite mitigation plans not being achieved in full
findings.detail: Adult Social Care care packages are forecast to overspend by £11.684m on a budget of £61.161m, reaching £72.845m outturn. The overspend affects all care types: Residential Care, Supported Living, Homecare and Nursing Care. The council's comments indicate that planned budget mitigations have not been achieved in full, meaning cost savings that were planned for in the year did not materialise.
findings.matters: Adult Social Care overspends are sector-wide, but the scale of this one and the failure of mitigation plans would interest finance directors at other councils facing similar pressures and lenders assessing financial resilience.
findings.figures: Budget £61.161m, forecast outturn £72.845m, overspend £11.684m
findings.quote: Pressure across all types of care packages - Residential Care, Supported Living ,Homecare & Nursing Care and budget mitigations not achieved in full

findings.headline: EFS loan drawdown deferred to year-end and only drawn if necessary; council may avoid drawdown by deploying reserves instead, to the extent available
findings.detail: The EFS is structured as a loan facility drawn only at year-end if needed, rather than as an upfront grant. The council has the option to use reserves to cover the deficit, which would avoid drawing the full £12.9m loan. The phrase "to the extent they are available" signals reserve levels may be constrained.
findings.matters: This raises two questions for a lender: the level of reserves available to deploy, and whether the council will need the full £12.9m despite the option to use reserves. Reserve depletion is a critical constraint on future financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £12.9m potential EFS drawdown in 2026/27; may be avoided if reserves permit
findings.quote: Actual draw down of the Loan Facility is at year end and only if needed – may be avoided by utilising Reserves instead (to the extent they are available)

findings.headline: EFS approval made in principle for 2026/27 only, conditional on external assurance review of council's financial position and governance arrangements
findings.detail: The EFS is described as an "In Principle" decision for 2026/27 only. Before a final capitalisation direction can be issued, the council must undergo an external assurance review assessing its financial position and governance arrangements. This signals government concerns about the council's financial controls and governance.
findings.matters: The conditional nature and limited duration of EFS approval signal that government has material concerns about this council's governance and management. This is relevant to lenders assessing credit risk and to finance directors assessing peer management quality.
findings.figures: £12.9m EFS for 2026/27 only (in principle); external assurance review required before final direction
findings.quote: in order for the department to provide a final capitalisation direction, the council is required to undergo an external assurance review which will include, but will not be limited to, an assessment of the council's financial position and governance arrangements

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget legally balanced via EFS loan facility, but structural deficit of £39.7m identified for 2027/28 requiring difficult decisions
findings.detail: While the council achieved a legally balanced 2026/27 budget through EFS, the presentation identifies a structural deficit of £39.7m for 2027/28 that will require difficult decisions. This signals that EFS was a one-year bridge, not a solution to the underlying problem.
findings.matters: The headline about balancing the budget masks the fact that a larger deficit looms next year. This council's financial pressures are not solved by EFS; the core structural challenge grows.
findings.figures: £39.7m structural deficit for 2027/28
findings.quote: Address the underlying structural deficit which for 2027/28 is £39.7m. Will require difficult decisions.

findings.headline: Government funding reduction of £13.8m per annum identified over three-year period from 2026/27 to 2028/29, with the largest cuts falling in outer years
findings.detail: The council faces a stepped reduction in central government funding beginning at £3.1m in 2026/27, then a further £10m reduction by 2028/29, totalling £13.8m per annum lost over the period. This represents a structural income loss underlying the council's deficit, with the trajectory worsening in outer years.
findings.matters: This documents a major structural income loss that cannot be controlled locally. The acceleration of cuts in outer years signals further budget challenges ahead even if other pressures stabilise.
findings.figures: £3.1m per annum from 2026/27; further £10m per annum reduction by 2028/29; total £13.8m per annum reduction over three-year period
findings.quote: Reduction in Government Funding of £3.1m per annum from 2026/27 – which will get significantly worse over the following 2-years with a further £10m per annum reduction by 2028/29. Total £13.8m per annum reduction in the annual funding from the government over a 3-year period.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care escalation of £14.8m, waste contract doubling of £6.5m, and government funding reduction of £3.1m per annum identified as three key drivers of structural deficit
findings.detail: The presentation identifies the immediate causes of the council's financial pressures. Adult Social Care costs escalated in 2025/26 and are expected to continue; the waste contract doubled in cost; and government funding is reducing. Understanding whether these pressures are specific to this council or systemic is relevant to assessing both local management performance and the sustainability of the broader financial problem.
findings.matters: Finance directors elsewhere need to know whether similar pressures are hitting them; lenders need to assess whether these costs are within the council's control or structural to the sector.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care £14.8m (21% of deficit); Waste Contract £6.5m; Government funding reduction £3.1m per annum from 2026/27
findings.quote: Rapidly escalating costs of Adult Social Care in 2025/26 which were anticipated to continue into 2026/27 - £14.8m (21%). Doubling in cost of the Waste Contract - £6.5m. Reduction in Government Funding of £3.1m per annum from 2026/27

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support borrowing requirement escalates from £12.9m in 2026/27 to £66.3m in 2029/30, totalling £175.3m over four years
findings.detail: The council set out EFS borrowing requirements across a four-year period, rising significantly year-on-year. The associated borrowing costs total £35.0m over the same period. The escalating requirement indicates the underlying structural deficit worsens substantially beyond 2026/27.
findings.matters: A lender and finance directors elsewhere need to see the medium-term debt trajectory. This council's structural problem is not a one-year issue; the required borrowing grows substantially as outer-year deficits emerge.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Property portfolio management lacks appropriate software system, strategic documentation, and proper filing controls
findings.detail: The Property Value for Money audit (Corporate Services) received a 'limited assurance' rating due to high-risk issues: lack of an appropriate software system to manage the portfolio (also flagged in 2024/25), gaps in records, and files stored on personal drives rather than shared folders—most significantly for rent reviews. A replacement system is anticipated by mid-2026. The council also lacks strategic documentation covering its approach to property portfolio management.
findings.matters: Weak property management controls over a material corporate asset (particularly rent reviews) indicate inability to realize value from the council's property portfolio and risk of lease arrangements that do not protect the council's interests. This is a balance-sheet matter for lenders.
findings.figures: Replacement software system anticipated by mid-2026
findings.quote: High risk issues were identified regarding the current lack of an appropriate software system (also highlighted in the 2024/25 Internal Audit Annual Report) to manage the portfolio, with related high-risk issues identified regarding gaps in records and filing of records on personal drives, rather than shared folders, most significantly in relation to rent reviews.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Limited assurance on Personal Assistance: 26 of 189 active PAs have expired DBS checks, two confirmed in sample
findings.detail: The Personal Assistance audit (Adult Services) received a 'limited assurance' rating. Testing found 26 of 189 active Personal Assistants recorded in the system had expired DBS checks. Sample testing of 10 records confirmed expired DBS checks in two instances. The service implemented immediate corrective actions, but this finding flags inadequate vetting controls over individuals providing care to vulnerable adults.
findings.matters: Expired DBS checks on personal care assistants indicate breakdown in safeguarding control over vulnerable adults. For a lender, this signals weak compliance with duty of care and child/adult protection frameworks, with potential reputational and legal liability.
findings.figures: 26 of 189 active PAs flagged as expired; sample of 10 confirmed 2 with expired checks
findings.quote: Of the 189 active PAs recorded in the Council's software system 26 are flagged as having expired DBS checks, with sample testing of a sample of ten confirming expired DBS checks in two instances.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Resource constraints worsening and contributing to audit findings; likely to continue through 2026/27
findings.detail: The CIA reports that 'resource constraints continue to be a contributing factor to a number of issues identified' and that 'the shortfall in resources and the resulting impact have worsened during 2025/26; a trend which is likely to continue through 2026/27.' The s151 Officer and committee will be informed if this impacts the ability to meet statutory audit requirements. Specialist IT audit skills are particularly limited (only 2 qualified officers).
findings.matters: Resource constraints that are worsening and expected to persist signal that the council is unable to fund or retain the capacity needed to maintain control environment strength. Combined with financial deterioration, this creates a negative feedback loop for control effectiveness.
findings.figures: Only 2 officers qualified in specialist IT auditing; training underway for third, fourth being identified
findings.quote: Resource constraints continue to be a contributing factor to a number of issues identified. The shortfall in resources and the resulting impact have worsened during 2025/26; a trend which is likely to continue through 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Council's financial position deteriorating with exceptional funding support granted for recovery
findings.detail: The annual opinion explicitly states that at the organisational level, 'the Council's financial position continues to deteriorate, with exceptional funding support having been granted, to support the Council's recovery.' This exceptional support sits alongside resource constraints that are themselves worsening and expected to persist through 2026/27.
findings.matters: Deteriorating financial position requiring exceptional government funding is the baseline indicator for lender risk. It directly affects both repayment capacity and the environment in which service delivery controls operate.
findings.figures: Exceptional funding support granted (amount not disclosed in this document)
findings.quote: At the organisational level the Council's financial position continues to deteriorate, with exceptional funding support having been granted, to support the Council's recovery.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Audit recommendation closure at 47% in 2025/26, compared to 55% in 2024/25, ending seven-year improvement trend with 3 high-risk and 2 medium-risk findings still open
findings.detail: Of 42 medium and higher-risk audit exceptions followed up during 2025/26, only 47% were closed, with 53% still in progress or open. This represents the first deterioration after seven years of gradual improvement during the Portsmouth partnership, with high-risk findings still open (3 of 25) and medium-risk findings still open (2 of 14).
findings.matters: Inability to implement audit recommendations signals weakness in management capacity to remediate control weaknesses. This trend reversal after sustained improvement is a red flag for a lender or finance director assessing management's ability to manage recovery.
findings.figures: 47% closed (2025/26) vs 55% closed (2024/25); 3 high-risk, 2 medium-risk, 1 low-risk exceptions still open; 53% of exceptions in progress or open
findings.quote: With 47% closed, compared to 55% in 2024/25. This ends the trend of gradual improvements observed during the seven years of the partnership with Portsmouth City Council.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Control environment deteriorating despite maintaining 'reasonable assurance' opinion
findings.detail: The CIA notes deterioration in the control environment in 2025/26: one audit produced 'no assurance' (none in 2024/25), the first critical risk finding has appeared (0 in 2024/25), and the number of medium-risk findings rose from 31 to 38. The council is explicitly described as 'an organisation under increased stress' and the CQC assessment of Adult Services rated it as 'requires improvement'.
findings.matters: An audit opinion that masks deteriorating underlying control strength is of particular concern to lenders. The direction of travel—not just the current state—matters for financial stability assessment.
findings.figures: Critical risk: 0 (2024/25) to 1 (2025/26); Medium risk findings: 31 (2024/25) to 38 (2025/26); No assurance audits: 0 (2024/25) to 1 (2025/26)
findings.quote: Taken together these all indicate an organisation under increased stress, which has and will continue to have an impact on the effectiveness of the control environment.

findings.paper_title: 7b. Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Critical audit finding on £600k EHCP direct payments with no approval, setup or monitoring controls
findings.detail: The Education Health Care Plans (EHCPs) audit resulted in a 'no assurance' opinion, the only such rating this year. Testing found that approximately £600,000 spent on direct payments lacked approval, setup, monitoring and auditing, with the risk of error or fraud assessed as 'very high'. Additionally, 31% of EHCP decisions in the sample were not made within the required six-week deadline.
findings.matters: This represents a critical control weakness in a high-value spending area with unmitigated fraud risk. Lenders rely on robust controls over discretionary payments, and a council unable to approve or monitor £600k of commitments signals fundamental control environment weakness.
findings.figures: £600,000 spent on direct payments; 31% of sample decisions missed six-week deadline
findings.quote: In 2024/25 approximately £600,000 was spent on direct payments, with sample testing identifying a lack of approval, setup, monitoring and auditing the risk of error/fraud being assessed as very high.

findings.headline: Council's audit recovery one year behind NAO LARRIG 01 schedule; qualified opinion now expected 2026/27 instead of 2025/26
findings.detail: The council was expected to recover to qualified opinion by 2025/26, but is now only one year into recovery from 2024/25 baseline. This delay was caused by limited procedures in 2022/23 and again in 2023/24 when the council 'failed to produce 2023/24 accounts in accordance with its planned timetable'.
findings.matters: Delayed recovery from disclaimer opinions extends the period of financial statement unreliability; falling behind schedule indicates persistent control and capacity issues.
findings.figures: Expected recovery: 2025/26 qualified opinion now delayed to 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council's progress is one year behind the expected timescales set out in LARRIG 01. This is because limited procedures were completed in 2022/23, and then again in 2023/24 when the Council failied to produce 2023/24 accounts in accordance with its planned timetable.

findings.headline: Pension Fund financial statements were not published by the statutory 30 June 2025 deadline, and working papers were of poor quality.
findings.detail: The Pension Fund accounts missed the Accounts and Audit Regulations deadline. Auditors reported that working papers were not of acceptable standard, primarily due to recent changes in the Pension Fund's key finance team. Significant delays occurred in obtaining supporting documentation and evidence.
findings.matters: Pension Fund accounting delays and quality issues reflect management capacity constraints; timeliness failures create regulatory compliance risk.
findings.figures: Deadline missed: 30 June 2025; team changes: recent
findings.quote: The financial statements were not published by the 30th June 2025 deadline set out in the Accounts and Audit Regulations. The quality of working papers and supporting evidence provided was generally not of an acceptable standard. This was primarily due to recent changes within the Pension Fund's key finance team.

findings.headline: IFRS 16 Leases implementation remains incomplete; management could not assess voluntary controlled schools adoption in time.
findings.detail: Auditors identified a £790k overstatement in peppercorn leases and £604k in PFI remeasurement differences. Management was unable to complete an assessment of whether voluntary controlled schools should be recognized on the balance sheet in IFRS 16, and these items could not be resolved before the backstop date.
findings.matters: Incomplete lease accounting indicates control environment weakness; unresolved assessments mean potential future restatement risk.
findings.figures: £790k peppercorn lease overstatement; £604k PFI remeasurement difference
findings.quote: Management have not been able to complete this assessment in sufficient time before the backstop date. Other misstatements identified related to overstatement of lease liabilities related to peppercorn leases (£790k overstatement) and a remeasurement difference in PFI lease liabilities (604k overstatement).

findings.headline: Property, Plant & Equipment valuations contain material errors and the Fixed Asset Register was not completed before draft accounts publication.
findings.detail: Auditors identified £3.7m overstatement between valuers' reports and the FAR, £980k misclassification between asset categories, and £130k net understatement. The FAR was not finalized before the 30 June draft publication, and auditors were unable to fully complete work on material assets under construction before the backstop date.
findings.matters: PPE represents a material asset class; unresolved valuation errors and process failures (late FAR completion) indicate weak asset accounting controls.
findings.figures: £3.7m overstatement (valuers vs FAR); £980k misclassification; £130k net understatement
findings.quote: Other misstatements identified related to overstatement of lease liabilities related to peppercorn leases (£790k overstatement) and a remeasurement difference in PFI lease liabilities (604k overstatement). Furthermore, we were not able to fully complete our work on material assets under construction balances in sufficient time before the backstop.

findings.headline: Adult social care and children's services overspend is persistent and unsustained, consuming corporate contingency.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 budget required a £7m release of corporate contingency to offset overspends in adult social care and children's services. In 2025/26, the Q1 forecast already shows a £3.4m overspend (1.6% of budget), again primarily driven by these service areas, and the council expects to use the entire £4m corporate contingency.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled demand-led service pressures indicate loss of budget control in the council's largest expenditure areas; the corporate contingency is a one-time buffer and cannot be relied upon.
findings.figures: 2024/25: £7m released from contingency; 2025/26 Q1: £3.4m overspend forecast; contingency available: £4m
findings.quote: A revised budget was approved at Full Council in February 2025 and included a release of £7m of the corporate contingency to offset the pressures in adult social care and children's services.

findings.headline: General Reserves are maintained at only £10.6m, providing minimal headroom above the £8m minimum level.
findings.detail: The council's reserves position shows only £2.6m of headroom above the Section 151 officer's minimum of £8m. The auditor describes this as 'very modest level of headroom'. The council has drawn £1.2m in 2024/25 and projects further drawdowns of £700k in 2028/29.
findings.matters: Thin reserve coverage limits the council's ability to absorb financial shocks or delayed savings delivery; any adverse variance in the MTFS could force service cuts.
findings.figures: General Reserves £10.6m; minimum level £8m; headroom £2.6m
findings.quote: General Reserves are maintained over the latest MTFS period at not lower than £10.6m, providing a very modest level of headroom to be able to respond to the risks associated with the future cost and funding uncertainty.

findings.headline: Annual savings requirements rise from £2.5m in 2026/27 to £6.5m in 2028/29, an increase of £2m per annum on prior years
findings.detail: The updated MTFS shows savings needs increasing from £2m per annum to £6.5m per annum by 2028/29. The council has a track record of meeting savings targets, but the scale and acceleration of requirements creates delivery risk, particularly given current governance issues.
findings.matters: Escalating, unmet savings requirements are a leading indicator of financial distress; failure to deliver would require further reserve drawdowns or service cuts.
findings.figures: 2026/27: £2.5m; 2028/29: £6.5m (another £2m per annum on prior years)
findings.quote: The MTFS update for 2025/26 to 2028/29 showed an increase in the annual savings requirement to £2.5m in 2026/27, and increasing further to £6.5m in 2028/29, i.e. another £2m per annum.

findings.headline: The council applied for Exceptional Financial Support of £12.9m for 2026/27 due to escalating cost pressures.
findings.detail: The EFS application indicates the council cannot balance its budget without exceptional government support. This follows a £1.2m drawdown from reserves in 2024/25 and reflects ongoing pressures in adult social care and children's services that are not being contained within budget.
findings.matters: EFS applications signal financial distress and dependency on government support; lenders view this as increased credit risk.
findings.figures: £12.9m EFS applied for 2026/27 (support agreed-in-principle)
findings.quote: For 2026/27 we noted that due to increasing costs pressures the Council has applied for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of £12.9m (support agreed-in-principle).

findings.headline: Auditors identified a significant weakness in governance arrangements, including inappropriate member behaviour, breaches of codes of conduct, and dysfunction affecting decision-making.
findings.detail: An independent governance review commissioned by the council found inappropriate behaviour at meetings, poor officer/member interface, lack of support to members, and policies not being used to address breaches. MHCLG expressed concerns about a 17 September 2025 meeting and the potential for a best value notice or inspection. The review concluded this has been 'symptomatic of dysfunction'.
findings.matters: Governance dysfunction directly affects financial decision-making quality, increases reputational risk, and creates potential for regulatory intervention and best value inspection.
findings.figures: Meeting of concern: 17 September 2025; review date: November 2025
findings.quote: Time and resources are being taken up by these issues, including unquantifiable costs of time, reputational damage, and delays in decision making that could have financial implications. The independent report concluded it has been symptomatic of dysfunction.

findings.headline: Auditors issued a disclaimer of opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements, with no reasonable assurance over material balances and movements.
findings.detail: Following a disclaimer on 2023/24, auditors lack assurance over opening balances from the prior year and all 2024/25 in-year movements and comparatives. The shortfall stems from incomplete evidence gathering and the statutory backstop date. This is the second consecutive year of disclaimer opinion.
findings.matters: Lenders cannot rely on the audited accounts for credit assessment; the council's financial position is materially uncertain.
findings.figures: 2024/25 and 2023/24 both issued disclaimer opinions; progress is one year behind LARRIG 01 schedule.
findings.quote: we are unable to conclude that the 2024/25 financial statements are free from material and pervasive misstatement of the financial statements. We therefore issued a disclaimer 2024/25 audit opinion.

findings.headline: Council has provided £5m credit facility commitment to Sovereign Network Homes
findings.detail: In June 2024, Isle of Wight Council joined other local authorities in establishing a credit facility for Sovereign Network Homes, committing £5m available for drawing over 3 years with optional 2-year extension. The council receives a non-utilization fee and interest at 2.5% above Bank of England base rate if drawn. As of end-December 2025, no funds have been drawn.
findings.matters: This creates contingent borrowing exposure: if SNH draws on the facility, the council's debt increases by up to £5m. It also represents credit risk exposure to an external organization.
findings.figures: £5m committed facility, currently undrawn
findings.quote: the council has agreed to provide a £5m credit facility for Sovereign Network Homes. This facility is for a period of 3 years with the option of an extension for a further two years.

findings.headline: Council must exit £37.1m commercial property investments before taking additional borrowing
findings.detail: The council holds £37.1m in commercial investments for financial return, purchased before the 2021 CIPFA Code restricted such borrowing. The treasury strategy requires review of exit options for these assets before the council can undertake further additional borrowing, effectively constraining access to new capital funding.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether capital funding plans are constrained by forced asset sales or borrowing restrictions. This dependency indicates compliance pressure and potential impact on capital spend.
findings.figures: £37.1m in commercial investments held for financial return
findings.quote: Before undertaking further additional borrowing the council will review the options for exiting these investments.

findings.headline: Council cash liquidity falls £7.8m short of its self-imposed three-month buffer target
findings.detail: As of 31 December 2025, cash available within 3 months was £24.0m against the council's target of £31.8m. This failure to meet the council's own voluntary liquidity measure suggests reduced cash flexibility to handle unexpected payments or expenditure.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence the council maintains adequate liquid reserves to meet obligations during market stress. Falling 25% short of self-imposed buffers signals cash management tightness.
findings.figures: Actual cash available £24.0m, target £31.8m, shortfall £7.8m
findings.quote: Total cash available within 3 months 24.0 31.8 No

findings.headline: Investment interest rates declining from 4.58% to 3.99% as economic environment softens
findings.detail: The average rate earned on the council's investment portfolio has fallen significantly over nine months, reflecting an environment of falling interest rates, despite investment holdings increasing by £4m.
findings.matters: Declining investment yields will reduce treasury gains available to offset budget pressures going forward; the council's ability to use treasury performance to mitigate deficits is diminishing.
findings.figures: Investment rate declined from 4.58% to 3.99%; investment holdings increased £4m
findings.quote: Over the period of this report the average interest rates on investments, have decreased from an average of 4.58% to 3.99%.

findings.headline: Council holds loans to two other local authorities as part of treasury strategy
findings.detail: The council is holding loans advanced to two other councils as part of its investment portfolio. The council monitors their financial position and avoids lending to any authority that has issued a S114 notice.
findings.matters: Represents counterparty concentration risk; loss of either borrower would mean loss of both principal and income. The mention of S114 notice monitoring suggests awareness of council financial stress in the sector.
findings.figures: Loans to 2 local authorities (specific amounts not disclosed)
findings.quote: In addition to investing in money market funds the council has loans advanced to two other local authorities. Close attention is taken to the financial situation of other local authorities, and no loans have been made to any authority that has issued a S114 notice.

findings.headline: £2.9 million treasury gain being used to offset wider council in-year budget pressures
findings.detail: Lower than budgeted borrowing costs and investment income combined to save £2.9m, which the council is deploying to help mitigate budget pressures across the wider authority. This reveals the council is managing in-year financial stress.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council is facing in-year budget pressures severe enough to require treasury gains as an offset, signalling potential structural budget stress.
findings.figures: £2.9 million saving; investment holdings increased £4m during nine-month period; borrowing costs lower than budget
findings.quote: The combination of reduced borrowing costs and increased investment income has resulted in a net forecast saving of £2.9 million contributing to mitigating wider council in-year budget pressures.

findings.paper_title: Item 6c - Full Council Potential Disposals Appendix 1 - Schedule of Potential Disposals
findings.headline: Newport Harbour regeneration previously investigated for housing but found not viable due to prohibitive infrastructure costs
findings.detail: The council previously investigated regeneration of Newport Harbour including substantial housing development but concluded it is not viable. Development would require extensive rebuilding of the harbour wall, but the cost is described as prohibitive. This leaves a significant strategic asset non-productive.
findings.matters: A major harbour-front asset remains unproductive due to identified but unresolved infrastructure cost barriers that prevent development or disposal
findings.figures: cost of harbour wall rebuilding described as prohibitive
findings.quote: To enable such development, extensive rebuilding of the harbour wall is required the cost of which is prohibitive

findings.paper_title: Item 6c - Full Council Potential Disposals Appendix 1 - Schedule of Potential Disposals
findings.headline: Multiple former municipal tips and contaminated sites carry environmental liabilities with uncertain remediation costs
findings.detail: The council holds several former municipal tips and contaminated sites including Stag Lane tip and East Yar Road tip. One site has 'little or no record of what is within the land.' Disposal of these sites is noted as subject to necessary site remediation, creating contingent costs.
findings.matters: Environmental liabilities on council-owned land create contingent costs and delay capital receipts until remediation is completed and disclosed
findings.figures: Multiple sites across Isle of Wight
findings.quote: Former municipal tip (little or no record of what is within the land)

findings.paper_title: Item 6c - Full Council Potential Disposals Appendix 1 - Schedule of Potential Disposals
findings.headline: Key disposals including Thompson House and Weston Academy are conditional on third-party decisions
findings.detail: Thompson House contracts are exchanged but conditional on Southern Water adopting a private drain; Weston Academy is exchanged conditional on planning consent. These major disposals have realization dependent on third parties and could fail to complete if conditions are not met.
findings.matters: Capital receipt timing and certainty is dependent on third-party actions beyond council control, creating risk to capital forecasting
findings.figures: 14 units at Thompson House; 16 units at Weston Academy
findings.quote: Contracts exchanged conditional upon Southern Water confirming the adoption of the existing private drain.

findings.paper_title: Item 6c - Full Council Potential Disposals Appendix 1 - Schedule of Potential Disposals
findings.headline: Shanklin Elmdon housing site experienced withdrawn offers after being marketed to developers
findings.detail: The site had received planning consent for 10 houses and was marketed to developers as part of the disposal pipeline. Developer offers were subsequently withdrawn and the council now needs to reconsider the approach. This signals market difficulty in disposing of planned housing sites.
findings.matters: Market rejection of housing development sites indicates pricing, demand, or viability challenges that could delay capital receipts or require write-down of value expectations
findings.figures: 10 houses (planning consent received)
findings.quote: The site has been marketed and a decision made to appoint a developer. However offers have been withdrawn and now need to reconsider the best way forward for this site.

findings.paper_title: Item 6c - Full Council Potential Disposals Appendix 1 - Schedule of Potential Disposals
findings.headline: Multiple housing development sites are being progressed through Council Housebuilding Support Fund without yet having assessed viability
findings.detail: Six sites are currently being progressed through CHSF to work toward planning consent and development, but viability has not yet been determined across multiple sites. Resources and grant funding are being committed to planning work before fundamental financial viability is established.
findings.matters: Capital commitments and grant-funded work are being initiated on sites without established viability, which is a governance concern for lenders assessing project discipline
findings.figures: 6 sites under CHSF consideration
findings.quote: Currently under consideration through Council Housebuilding Support Fund to work towards planning consent

findings.paper_title: Item 6c - Full Council Potential Disposals Appendix 1 - Schedule of Potential Disposals
findings.headline: Ryde Nicholson Road business park extension investment resulted in a major deficit after viability assessment
findings.detail: The council invested to secure planning application for employment-use development, but subsequent viability assessment found a major deficit. This represents a realized capital loss on a development project and raises questions about project evaluation and investment discipline.
findings.matters: Historical capital losses on development projects indicate investment risk and governance concerns about project evaluation and approvals
findings.figures: major deficit (amount not specified)
findings.quote: Investment undertaken to secure planning application (predominantly employment), but subsequent viability assessment resulted in a major deficit.

findings.headline: PFI contract costs escalate from £1.1m to £5.9m annually by 2030-31, creating compressed future revenue budgets
findings.detail: PFI Contract Costs total £18.1m over six years, rising steeply from £1.1m in 2025-26 to £5.9m in 2030-31. Costs more than double in three years (2025-26 to 2028-29) and continue climbing. These are revenue commitments that compound the impact of capital borrowing.
findings.matters: Escalating PFI payments reduce financial flexibility to respond to service pressures. Combined with unsupported borrowing debt service, rising PFI obligations constrain future budget options.

findings.headline: Coastal management spending jumps to £32.7m in 2026-27, a 21-fold increase from current year
findings.detail: Coastal Related Schemes total £34.5m over six years, but spending accelerates from £1.5m in 2025-26 to £32.7m in 2026-27. The magnitude and concentration suggest either a major coastal defence scheme or acceleration of erosion/flood-related works.
findings.matters: Isle of Wight faces material coastal erosion and flood risk. Understanding whether this spending reflects deferred maintenance, escalating climate impacts, or a one-off major scheme informs whether elevated capital and revenue costs will persist.

findings.headline: Affordable Housing scheme front-loads £35.4m capital investment into 2026-27, the single largest capital commitment
findings.detail: Affordable Housing totals £37.9m over six years, but £35.4m falls in 2026-27. This scheme alone drives a significant portion of the unsupported borrowing spike and will create ongoing debt service costs.
findings.matters: A lender evaluates whether this scale of housing investment is commercially sound and whether the council can service the debt while managing other pressures or service deficits.

findings.headline: Unsupported borrowing concentrates in 2026-27 at £51.1m, representing 72% of the six-year total
findings.detail: The council's £70.5m unsupported borrowing is heavily front-loaded: £51.1m in 2026-27 alone, compared to £10.5m in 2025-26. Borrowing drops sharply thereafter (£5m in 2027-28, £0.7m in 2028-29). This concentration creates acute debt service pressure in one year.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether the council can finance a £51m spike while maintaining reserves and service delivery. This affects future borrowing capacity and financial headroom to handle service pressures.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care costs are forecast to grow 43% over five years from £75.1m to £107.5m.
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is the largest budget area and is growing at approximately 7.4% annually, significantly outpacing inflation. The projected £32.4m increase is the single largest driver of overall expenditure growth from £217.3m to £304.8m.
findings.matters: Rapidly growing adult social care costs indicate demographic or service pressures that will continue to strain the council's finances and drive the need for external support.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care, Public Health & Housing: £75.1m (2025/26) to £107.5m (2029/30), an increase of £32.4m or 43%

findings.headline: Isle of Wight is planning to rely on exceptional financial support growing to £66.3m by 2029/30, representing 22% of total council revenue.
findings.detail: The council's budget assumes exceptional financial support from government that grows from zero in 2025/26 to £12.9m in the 2026/27 original budget, then accelerates in forecasts to £39.7m, £56.4m, and £66.3m. This is not a standard revenue source and its rapid expansion indicates the council cannot balance its budget through normal financing alone.
findings.matters: Reliance on exceptional financial support of this scale signals structural financial distress and raises questions about sustainability and whether this support will continue. A lender needs to know whether a quarter of the council's revenues depend on discretionary government funding.

findings.paper_title: Item 6c - Full Council Report - Land Property Asset Disposal Considerations
findings.headline: Grant deadline of 31 March 2026 creates time pressure that may override normal project evaluation discipline
findings.detail: The council received the Council Housebuilding Support Fund grant in mid-November 2025 with a hard spend deadline of 31 March 2026—a compressed eight-month window. The report notes that failing to approve this schedule risks losing the grant entirely, making the deadline the driver of the decision rather than project readiness. This compressed timeline may not allow adequate due diligence on site viability.
findings.matters: Time-driven funding decisions can bypass proper financial scrutiny. Lenders are concerned when councils approve capital commitments primarily to avoid losing grants rather than because projects are properly evaluated.
findings.figures: £210,000 grant; received mid-November 2025; must spend by 31 March 2026
findings.quote: received mid November 2025 and to be spent by 31 March 2026

findings.paper_title: Item 6c - Full Council Report - Land Property Asset Disposal Considerations
findings.headline: No viability assessment has been completed and schemes are acknowledged as potentially unviable without additional subsidy
findings.detail: The report states explicitly that 'viability testing yet been undertaken on the six sites' and warns that 'social rent housing schemes may not be viable without additional financial support'. Delivery is contingent on securing access to future central government funding (a £39 billion Social and Affordable Homes Programme) which has not yet been confirmed available or that the council will access.
findings.matters: A council advancing sites through planning without first confirming financial viability risks committing capital and staff effort to schemes that cannot be delivered, particularly problematic when linked to diverted revenue resources.
findings.figures: £39 billion proposed Social and Affordable Homes Programme (date of launch not confirmed)
findings.quote: social rent housing schemes may not be viable without additional financial support

findings.paper_title: Item 6c - Full Council Report - Land Property Asset Disposal Considerations
findings.headline: The council is diverting property staff from revenue-generating work to unpaid housing delivery, with no permanent staffing solution beyond the grant deadline
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that professional support for housing work is 'met from within existing resources' and 'does impact on other property development work such as the generation of revenue income, delivery of regeneration schemes and existing capital receipt disposals'. The grant funding ends 31 March 2026, after which this work has no identified funding, leaving a gap in both capacity and revenue generation.
findings.matters: Councils rely heavily on property disposal revenue to fund capital investment. Diverting property staff to non-revenue-generating housing schemes directly reduces capital receipts and constrains future capital spending capacity.
findings.figures: £150,000 allocated to PBH; £60,000 to external support; no ongoing funding identified
findings.quote: the professional support service work being undertaken by the property services team is met from within existing resources, although this can and does impact on other property development work such as the generation of revenue income, delivery of regeneration schemes and existing capital receipt disposals

findings.paper_title: Item 6c - Full Council Report - Land Property Asset Disposal Considerations
findings.headline: Planning costs on six sites will likely reach £240,000 but only £150,000 has been allocated, creating a funding shortfall
findings.detail: The council's planning consultant estimates that bringing each site to planning application stage will cost approximately £40,000, yet only £150,000 of the £210,000 grant has been allocated to this work. The report acknowledges this will be insufficient to bring all six sites to full planning application stage, meaning either sites will be abandoned mid-process or additional funding will be needed.
findings.matters: Underfunded project pipelines often result in write-offs or repeated funding requests, both of which indicate poor project evaluation discipline.
findings.figures: £40,000 per site estimate; £150,000 allocated; £210,000 total grant
findings.quote: Based on PBH estimates, the likely cost to bring each site to the planning application stage will be circa £40,000

findings.paper_title: Item 6c - Full Council Report - Land Property Asset Disposal Considerations
findings.headline: No capital funding has been identified for housebuilding on any of the six sites despite committing to housing delivery
findings.detail: The council has secured £210,000 in revenue grant funding to advance six residential sites through the planning process. However, the report explicitly states that actual housebuilding requires capital funding (either external grant or council borrowing/capital reserves) which has not been identified. The schemes may also not be viable without additional financial support.
findings.matters: A council committing to housing delivery without identifying capital funding signals either projects will stall after planning or future capital reserves will be absorbed into delivery, limiting other investment.
findings.figures: £210,000 revenue grant; no capital identified
findings.quote: no capital monies have been identified for housebuilding 'by or for the council'

findings.paper_title: Item 6a - Full Council Budget Report Feb 2026
findings.headline: Already delivered £101m in savings over 15 years (40% of controllable spend); remaining savings pool is depleted
findings.detail: The council has made £101m in savings since 2011/12. It is now proposing £6.3m more (£4.1m ongoing + £2.2m pension). The council states it has exhausted efficiency options and that further savings will require service reductions. This is the 16th consecutive year of budget cuts.
findings.matters: A council that has already cut 40% of controllable spending has no efficiency reserves left. Future savings will be achieved only through service cuts, which may breach statutory duties or reduce council's ability to function.
findings.figures: £101m cumulative savings 2011/12-2026/27; £6.3m new savings proposed 2026/27; only 5% of £4.1m savings target is service reduction
findings.quote: Since 2011/12, savings of £101m will have already been made (over 40% of controllable spend) due to the combination of government funding reductions and increasing demographic cost pressures

findings.paper_title: Item 6a - Full Council Budget Report Feb 2026
findings.headline: Forecast structural deficits of £39m (2027/28), £55m (2028/29), £65m (2029/30) if no transformation plan succeeds
findings.detail: The council's medium-term forecast shows deficits compounding annually. By 2029/30, cumulative EFS debt would reach £172m with annual debt servicing costs of £17m. These forecasts assume successful savings delivery, which is highly uncertain given the scale of Social Care and Waste pressures.
findings.matters: Deficits of this scale, if not reversed, indicate an unsustainable council. The forecast assumes savings that may not be deliverable and does not account for further unforeseen cost shocks.
findings.figures: £20m structural deficit 2026/27; £39m 2027/28; £55m 2028/29; £65m 2029/30; cumulative debt £172m; debt service costs £17m p.a. by 2029/30
findings.quote: Left unattended and without the implementation of a Transformation Plan (and Improvement Board) which should include continued lobbying of Central Government for Fair Funding for the Island, the 'Structural Deficit' is forecast to rise to £65m by 2029/30, representing 21% of the Council's total net spending.

findings.paper_title: Item 6a - Full Council Budget Report Feb 2026
findings.headline: Medium-term capital planning abandoned; £6.8m of approved schemes deleted to fund budget gap
findings.detail: The council's previous three-year capital investment pipeline has been scrapped. Approved capital schemes of £6.8m have been deleted and new capital investment rationed to only health/safety, business critical, or high-value schemes. This is a one-time funding source that cannot be repeated.
findings.matters: Loss of capital investment in IT, fleet, buildings, and infrastructure means service deterioration over time. The one-off measure buys time but reduces service sustainability.
findings.figures: £6.8m capital schemes deleted; £2.2m surplus capital resources released; £17.5m total new capital investment for 2026/27 (down from previous pipeline)
findings.quote: Regrettably, due to the need to minimise debt support from EFS and remove any non-essential planned capital investments, the Council has had to abandon its previous medium term approach to Capital Planning which aimed to provide surety of funding for the next 3 years for the Council's core essential service delivery (including necessary and desirable IT infrastructure and improvement, Vehicle Fleet plus Health and Safety Requirements for operational buildings).

findings.paper_title: Item 6a - Full Council Budget Report Feb 2026
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £27.1m; £4.6m liability falls to general fund from March 2028
findings.detail: Schools high needs (SEND) deficit is forecast at £27.1m by March 2026. While government will cover 90% from March 2028 onwards, the council's residual liability is £4.6m. This is not yet factored into the 2027/28+ forecasts, representing a hidden future cost.
findings.matters: Hidden liability that crystallises after the immediate budget crisis. Represents further structural deficit that will need to be funded through additional savings or borrowing.
findings.figures: £27.1m total DSG deficit; £4.6m council liability post-March 2028 (10% of forecast deficits); 90% government support assumed for existing deficit only
findings.quote: Based on receiving 90% support for the forecast DSG deficit to March 2026 of £27.1m and forecast future deficits for 2026/27 and 2027/28 in aggregate amounting to £18.8m also attracting 90% support, the overall liability that is estimated to fall to the Council once the statutory override comes to an end in March 2028 is £4.6m. At the time of writing, this further liability has not been factored into the Council's future forecasts.

findings.paper_title: Item 6a - Full Council Budget Report Feb 2026
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review removes £3.1m government funding in 2026/27, £13.4m over 3 years
findings.detail: Government's funding reform ('Fair Funding Review') redistributed funding based on relative need. Isle of Wight lost 16% of government funding over the period due to: (1) loss of a 'remoteness' factor estimated at £5m-£15m, and (2) deduction for high local Council Tax base. Multi-year settlement announced 09 Feb 2026.
findings.matters: Structural loss of government funding creates a permanent funding gap that cannot be closed by efficiency alone. This is driven by policy, not council performance, yet the council bears the full cost.
findings.figures: £3.1m reduction 2026/27; £13.4m cumulative loss 2026/27-2028/29; 16% reduction in funding settlement period; 15% loss of Core Spending Power (excl. Council Tax)
findings.quote: The Fair Funding Review has been extremely negative for the Council, being a reduction of 16% over the Settlement period... The absence of a 'Remoteness' factor being applied throughout the funding formulae (being applied to Adult Social Care only which represents 37.5% of the total allocation) - this is estimated to be a loss of circa. £15m by 2028/29 (£5m for 2026/27).

findings.paper_title: Item 6a - Full Council Budget Report Feb 2026
findings.headline: Waste contract doubled in cost overnight, adding £6.5m permanent new liability
findings.detail: The council's waste contract failed and repricing increased costs from ~£3m to £9m annually. This is treated as a permanent commitment going forward. No efficiency savings or demand reduction mechanism identified.
findings.matters: Contract failure causing 100%+ cost increase in a major service is a red flag for procurement risk and inability to manage supplier relationships. This cost will compound for years.
findings.figures: £6.5m increase in 2026/27; rising to £9m by 2027/28; permanent commitment
findings.quote: The doubling in cost of the Waste Contract - £6.5m

findings.paper_title: Item 6a - Full Council Budget Report Feb 2026
findings.headline: Adult Social Care costs jumped £14.8m (21% of structural deficit) with no permanent solution
findings.detail: Social Care overspends in 2025/26 totalled £8.8m driven by increasing numbers in care packages and escalating per-unit costs. The budget now locks in £14.8m additional spending for 2026/27, continuing to rise. The council extracts £2.3m via a Social Care Precept on Council Tax but this covers only 15% of the cost increase.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled demand growth in statutory Social Care services (70% of controllable spend) has exhausted the council's savings capacity. This is the primary driver of EFS and structural deficits.
findings.figures: £14.8m increase 2026/27; £8.8m overspend in 2025/26; Social Care represents ~70% of controllable spend; cost growth continues at ~10% p.a. forecast to 2029/30
findings.quote: The rapidly escalating costs of Adult Social Care in the current year, which are expected to continue into 2026/27 - £14.8m (21%)

findings.paper_title: Item 6a - Full Council Budget Report Feb 2026
findings.headline: Council cannot set a legal budget without £13m emergency government borrowing facility
findings.detail: Isle of Wight cannot balance its 2026/27 budget even after £6.3m of savings. Without Exceptional Financial Support (EFS), the S.151 Officer is required to issue a s.114 notice, triggering statutory spending controls and government intervention. This is described as 'the most challenging [budget] ever considered by the Council for the past 10 years'.
findings.matters: A council unable to set a budget without emergency government borrowing is in severe financial distress. S.114 notices are rare and indicate loss of control; they destabilise service delivery and organisation.
findings.figures: £13m EFS required; £20m structural deficit 2026/27; £65m by 2029/30; accumulated debt of £172m if all drawn
findings.quote: The Budget for 2026/27 will be the most challenging ever considered by the Council for the past 10 years. The Budget for 2026/27, prepared responsibly and with sufficient resilience, can only be considered to be a legal Budget if it incorporates a debt facility (which is only incurred if drawn upon) provided by Central Government and known as Exceptional Financial Support (EFS).

findings.headline: Service loan portfolio heavily impaired; £1.3m loss allowance against £1.5m outstanding (87% impairment rate)
findings.detail: The council's service loans, made primarily to local businesses for economic development, total £1.5m (2026/27 forecast) but carry a £1.3m loss allowance. Net figure shown in accounts is only £0.2m. The 87% impairment rate reflects either poor borrower credit quality or management's high assessment of default probability.
findings.matters: Loss allowances reflect expected defaults. An 87% impairment rate on the loan book suggests significant credit deterioration or very weak borrower capacity; material loan losses would impact reserves and revenue.
findings.figures: Outstanding service loans £1.5m (forecast 2026/27); Loss allowance £1.3m; Net figure £0.2m; Approved limit £35.0m
findings.quote: Accounting standards require the council to set aside a loss allowance for loans, reflecting the likelihood of non-payment.

findings.headline: Council building earmarked reserve to guard against property valuation losses and rental voids
findings.detail: Council is establishing a specific earmarked reserve over time as a safeguard against potential fair value deterioration of properties, loss of rental income, and property maintenance costs. This precautionary reserve-building suggests management concern about downside risks on the £37.2m portfolio.
findings.matters: Proactive reserve-building against identified risks (valuation loss, income loss, repair costs) indicates management's assessment that these risks are material and warrant pre-funding rather than paying as incurred.
findings.figures: Amount not specified; total property exposure £37.2m
findings.quote: The council maintains a specific earmarked reserve which is being built over time to a level sufficient to provide a safeguard against any difference in the fair value of the assets versus acquisition cost, any potential loss of rental income and future improvement works to properties.

findings.headline: Property valuations at material risk; council ready to restate if values fall significantly below cost
findings.detail: Annual property revaluation scheduled for March 2026. If fair values fall 'significantly below' purchase cost (£35.1m), the council will present an updated investment strategy to full council detailing revenue and security impacts. This contingency language indicates management awareness of downside valuation risk.
findings.matters: £37.2m property holdings represent 52% of total investments; material write-down would affect council's asset security, reserve adequacy, and potentially revenue budget if income falls.
findings.figures: Property portfolio book value £37.2m, purchase cost £35.1m; current net surplus £2.1m at risk
findings.quote: Should the 2025-26 year-end accounts preparation and audit process value these properties significantly below their purchase cost, then an updated investment strategy will be presented to full council, with the annual report on the performance of the commercial property investment portfolio detailing the impact of the loss on the security of investments and any revenue consequences arising therefrom.

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio frozen; council abandons £100m investment programme
findings.detail: Council previously approved expansion of commercial investments up to £100m but has now decided to cap holdings at current £37.2m across four properties (Salford £12.6m, Aylesford £8.5m, Oxford £12.3m, Southampton £3.8m). No further acquisitions planned. Management responsibility shifted from external Portsmouth City Council arrangement to in-house team.
findings.matters: Complete halt to a previously-approved expansion programme may indicate concerns about property market conditions, valuation risks, or loss of financial capacity to pursue the strategy.
findings.figures: Current portfolio £37.2m; previously approved limit £100m; four properties purchased 2018-19
findings.quote: the council does not intend to increase the size of its commercial property investment portfolio beyond the current holdings detailed above

findings.paper_title: Agenda item 8a Comment by S151 Officer
findings.headline: Potential unquantified capital commitments if Council pursues future Shareholder status.
findings.detail: If and when the Council transitions to Shareholder status, the pension fund may be required to commit a sizeable share capital sum to the pool company and potentially fund further capital calls to sustain it. These are conditional on future Shareholder status but flag potential future financial obligations.
findings.matters: Unquantified future capital commitments to a pension pool company could affect council finances and liquidity
findings.figures: None - described as 'sizeable' but not quantified
findings.quote: consideration of the pension fund committing to a sizeable share capital sum in the company and also potentially committing to fund further capital calls, if required to sustain the company

findings.paper_title: Agenda item 8a Comment by S151 Officer
findings.headline: S151 Officer warns non-compliance with pension scheme deadline risks Government intervention and independent governance review
findings.detail: The S151 Officer warns that non-compliance invites Government intervention and direct direction to join, which would be reputationally damaging and trigger an independent governance review under powers granted in the Pension Bill.
findings.matters: Government intervention and governance review would undermine council creditworthiness and investor confidence in management
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Should the Council not proceed to join with Client status, there is a serious risk that Government would intervene and direct the Council to join. This would be reputationally damaging to the Council and likely invite an independent review of a potential failure of governance.

findings.paper_title: Agenda item 8a Comment by S151 Officer
findings.headline: Governance arrangements insufficient for full Shareholder status; Council entering as Client only.
findings.detail: LGPS Central cannot offer Shareholder status due to compliance and financial risks. The Council lacks strengthened governance arrangements including appointment of a Senior Pensions Officer with appropriate delegations as required by regulatory standards. The S151 Officer identifies this as the blocking issue for Shareholder status.
findings.matters: Governance gaps are a compliance and reputation risk; Client-only status is lower-tier membership with limitations
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: requires strengthened Governance arrangements to be in place by the Isle of Wight Pension Fund (IWPF) in order to conform with regulatory requirements associated with Shareholder status. This includes demonstrating that minimum governance standards can be met including having appointed a Senior Pensions Officer with appropriate delegations

findings.paper_title: Agenda item 8a Comment by S151 Officer
findings.headline: Hard April 2026 compliance deadline for investment pool membership with 7-week delay from late November decision.
findings.detail: The Council must comply with pending Government legislation requiring investment pool membership by 1 April 2026. The decision to join LGPS Central came on 19 November 2025, creating a 7-week delay compared to the deadline. This late timing has constrained the Council to joining as Client rather than Shareholder.

findings.figures: Deadline: 1 April 2026; Decision date: 19 November 2025; Delay: 7 weeks
